Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6436. Human-Elephant Conflict Could Explode Across Southern Africa As Scientists Warn of a Growing Crisis

Human-elephant conflict could intensify across Southern Africa as expanding farmland and increasingly dry conditions reshape the landscape.

By 2085, the area of Southern Africa facing a high risk of elephant crop raids could expand by 33% to 100%, according to a new study. Researchers predict that growing human populations, expanding farmland, and increasingly dry conditions will intensify encounters between elephants and farmers, with human land use playing the largest role.

Southern Africa is home to more than 290,000 African savanna elephants (Loxodonta africana), representing roughly 70% of the continent’s savanna elephant population. As agricultural communities expand into elephant habitat, crop raids can destroy valuable harvests, threaten household incomes, and undermine local support for wildlife conservation.

To understand what causes these encounters, Evan Patrick and colleagues analyzed reported elephant crop raids from 2004 to 2020 across 38 communal conservancies in Namibia. They combined statistical methods designed to identify causal relationships with machine learning models that predict where conflicts are most likely to occur. Their analysis extended across a larger landscape encompassing northern Botswana and parts of Angola and Zambia.

“We find that human population growth, cropland expansion, and climate-driven aridity in core elephant-protected areas drive conflict risk,” the authors write.

Population growth was linked to higher crop-raiding rates during both wet and dry seasons, while expanding cropland and developed areas were associated with increased incidents during the wet season. Drier conditions within protected elephant habitats also predicted more wet-season raids in neighboring communities, suggesting that shortages of natural resources may push elephants toward agricultural land.

The researchers mapped potential conflict hotspots by examining vegetation cover, proximity to rivers, roads and wildlife fences, population density, and vegetation productivity. Tree cover and vegetation greenness were particularly influential predictors, while roads and fences appeared to shape where elephants encounter human settlements.

High-risk areas included regions north of Namibia’s Etosha National Park, the northeastern Zambezi Region, and parts of northern Botswana surrounding the Okavango Delta and Moremi Wildlife Reserve. Many of these landscapes connect important elephant habitats with areas used for farming.

Crop raids also showed pronounced seasonal differences. Historical records revealed that average incidents per mapped grid cell were more than ten times higher during the wet season than during the dry season, when agricultural activity and vegetation conditions differ.

Using projections of climate, population growth, and land use, the team modeled potential changes through 2085. All four scenarios predicted increasing crop-raiding activity and a wider distribution of high-risk areas, although the magnitude depended on future development patterns.

The greatest increases occurred under a scenario involving substantial population growth and land conversion, known as “regional rivalry.” Under this pathway, projected wet-season crop raiding was approximately twice as high as under the more sustainable development scenario. Even the scenario with the most severe climate impacts did not produce the highest conflict levels.

“Aggressive human land-use expansion leads to the most dramatic increases in conflict, with climate impacts playing a significant but smaller role,” the researchers explain.

Reference: “An expanding human footprint drives escalating human–elephant conflict across a transboundary African landscape through 2085” by Evan Patrick, Maxwell Pepperdine, Christy Yu, Sophie Pesek, Olivia Somhegyi, Joana M Krieger, Nickolas McManus, Ezequiel Fabiano, Colgar Sikopo, Patrick R Roehrdanz and Ashley Larsen, 7 July 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag205

#6435. Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Erin Garcia de Jesús, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.

It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.

He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.

The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.

“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

#6432. The Mystery of Hair Growth Patterns May Finally Have a Simple Explanation

A new study reveals how subtle interactions between cells and chemical signals may shape the intricate patterns of mammalian hair.

The precise arrangement of hair follicles across an animal’s skin may arise from a surprisingly simple process. Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have developed a mathematical model showing how cells responding to chemical signals can generate distinct hair patterns in two mammalian species, without requiring a complex system to determine where each follicle forms.

Published in PNAS, the research challenges a long-standing explanation for hair follicle development and suggests that variations in the same underlying cellular process could produce different patterns across species.

Hair follicles begin forming before birth in specialized embryonic structures called placodes. These structures also give rise to feathers and most types of scales. Their arrangement varies between species, but scientists have long debated how developing tissues establish such organized patterns.

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the prevailing explanation has been the expansion-induction model. According to this theory, each newly formed placode releases an inhibitory molecule that temporarily prevents others from developing nearby. As the skin expands, new areas move beyond the molecule’s influence, allowing additional placodes to form in the spaces between existing ones.

Although this model can account for the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, researchers have not experimentally established that it explains hair follicle organization more broadly across mammals.

A research team co-led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor in UNIGE’s Department of Genetics and Evolution, investigated a different mechanism called chemotaxis. This process allows cells to move in response to chemical gradients. It also helps white blood cells navigate toward areas of inflammation.

The researchers created a mathematical model in which mobile cells in the dermis respond to an attractive chemical signal produced by the epidermis, the skin’s outer layer. As the simulated embryonic skin grows, these interactions spontaneously produce placodes in patterns that closely match the developmental sequence observed in laboratory mice.

“Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form,” explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. “Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.”

The researchers next examined the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles form a highly regular, directionally organized pattern. Unlike the arrangement found in laboratory mice, this distinctive configuration cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental data obtained through three-dimensional imaging of embryonic skin, the team adapted its mathematical model to reflect the spiny mouse’s particular biochemical characteristics and skin growth patterns. The same chemotactic mechanism successfully reproduced the species’ characteristic follicle arrangement.

These simulations suggest that different mammalian hair patterns could emerge from a shared process governed by cell movement and chemical signaling, with species-specific differences in how those interactions unfold. The results provide a potential alternative to the conventional model, although mathematical agreement with observed patterns does not establish that chemotaxis is the mechanism operating in living skin.

“Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution,” concludes Athanasia Tzika. “The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.”

Reference: “Chemotactic self-organization captures the dynamics of mammalian hair follicle patterning” by Muhamet Ibrahimi, Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, Athanasia C. Tzika and Michel C. Milinkovitch, 2 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2530407123

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

#6430. The 7 Best Car Battery Chargers for Roadside Emergencies

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Maintain your car battery—or bring a dead one back to life.

The 12-volt battery is one of the least complex components in modern vehicles but one of the most crucial. If it’s not in good condition, the engine won’t start, and none of the vehicle’s fancy systems will work. Car batteries have a limited lifecycle and deteriorate with time. This can happen for many reasons, including extended inactivity, extreme temperatures, or even something as simple as accidentally leaving the lights on after you turn off the engine.

That’s why it’s handy to have an external car battery charger so your engine is ready to go when you need it. A charger can also help extend your battery's life, for instance, in a vehicle you don't drive often—a weekend getaway camper or an old classic cruiser. Some chargers also have a jumpstart feature, eliminating the need for jumper cables (and the inconvenience of a required second vehicle).

You might be surprised to hear that electric vehicles use the same 12-volt car batteries as their internal combustion counterparts. Regardless, modern vehicles rely on this ancillary battery to power lights and onboard electronics when the ignition is off. Here, we’ve compiled the best chargers for cars and motorcycles, including everything from a solar-powered charger to a model that can revive several vehicles at once.

Noco’s Genius 10, the brand’s flagship single-vehicle charger, offers many cool features, including the ability to “force charge” a battery so dead it won't generate any voltage when you hook it up. (Most modern chargers won’t do this.) Maintenance and “desulfation” modes extend your battery's useful life while keeping it ready to go.

Unlike smaller, less ambitious chargers, the Genius 10 charges a vehicle battery to full power in the shortest safe time. It can even charge the new generation of lithium-ion car batteries, like the complex, expensive units fitted to many newer BMWs.

All the basic features are here at a very low price, including protection from reverse clamping and a “float mode” for fully charged batteries.

The included set of bolt-on leads lets you quickly connect and disconnect the charger. Operation couldn’t be simpler: a green light shows the Motopower is on, and a red light indicates charging status. With 1.5 amps of power, it charges slightly faster than most competitors in the low-price bracket.

Think of this 15-amp charger as a miniature version of the shop-grade Schumacher. It’s also the form and function that will be most familiar to older or experienced users. The included clamps are high-quality and should fit most cars. Just clamp on, plug in, and select one of three modes.

The 15-amp rapid charge is slightly more than the competition can manage, and a carrying handle makes it easy to place where you want it.

This charger is compact, light, easy to operate, and almost bombproof. It delivers a 3-amp charge, then automatically switches to float mode to maintain proper voltage and prevent overcharging.

A two-color LED indicates charging status, and if the battery voltage drops below a certain level, it resumes full charging output in adaptive mode. It’s compatible with most automotive batteries and can switch between 6- and 12-volt batteries with the push of a button. Its battery clamps are spark-proof, and the Battery Tender 3-Amp will automatically detect reverse polarity. It comes with a 5-year warranty and lifetime customer service.

Dealerships and race shops that used to scatter CTEK individual chargers throughout the building are now switching to the multi-vehicle Noco 2x4 model. It weighs just under 8 pounds, mounts to a wall, and can handle four vehicles at the same time, each in a different mode.

Want to float charge one car, recondition another, and bring two other dead batteries back to life in force-charge mode? Not a problem.

If you own a vehicle you only drive occasionally, an under-the-hood charger saves the hassle of disconnecting it from the battery and storing it each time you want to go for a cruise.

The compact Schumacher SC1300 mounts under the hood to supply up to 1.5 amps, while a built-in microprocessor automatically adjusts the charging rate to maintain an ideal charge state. Float mode delivers a small current when needed.

Reverse hook-up protection prevents the charger from working if the battery clamps are installed in reverse polarity, and the Schumacher automatically detects 6-volt or 12-volt batteries.

If an electrical outlet isn’t available or if you just want to use the sun to keep your battery topped off, the Sun Energize solar-powered charger is a reliable option. It trickle-charges a variety of automotive batteries, as well as some lithium batteries.

A built-in charge controller prevents overcharging; charging stops when a battery is topped off and automatically resumes when it drains.

An LED indicator shows charge and battery conditions. The 20.1 x 13.8 x 0.7-inch solar panel is larger than the other chargers here, but it’s built to handle high winds and heavy loads and is IP65 waterproof.

We tested some external battery chargers under varying weather conditions, while others were chosen based on feedback from car enthusiast friends. The selections represent a wide variety of chargers with different capabilities to match a broad range of use cases. We have years of experience traveling the country with these chargers and know their performance very well.

If you store a vehicle for long periods, you’ll want a charger to keep the battery from fully dying and turning into a paperweight. (It’s also nice to know it will start without jumper cables.) But a battery charger can make a difference in plenty of other situations.

If you regularly experience below-freezing temperatures at night, a charger with a maintenance function can significantly extend your battery's life. If you rarely drive more than a few miles at a time, a charger can prevent your battery from discharging too far—leaving you with a no-start condition. Last but not least, older vehicles often struggle to recharge slightly depleted batteries on the move, so starting the day with a fully charged battery can also extend the life of your alternator and charging system.

Charging power is traditionally measured in amps. Think of amps as the amount of juice that can be put back into the battery at any given time; for example, a 10-amp charger puts twice as much charge into the battery as a 5-amp one. A quick stroll through a listing of battery chargers can be confounding, though. Some have 40 amps, and some have 0.75 amps, and yet they do the same thing. In reality, the difference is easy to understand. The more power a charger has, the more quickly it can bring a dead battery back to life. The tradeoff is cost, size, and weight.

If you’re charging a small motorcycle battery or maintaining a good-condition battery in a cherished collector car, then a 0.75-amp charger will do just fine. If you’re worried that your pickup won’t start in the winter, 2 to 10 amps is a better bet. Any capability above that is mostly for mechanics who need to quickly charge or recondition batteries in the shop.

Every charger here can “maintain” a charged battery, keeping it from slowly discharging between uses. Most chargers can also bring a depleted battery back up to full power. A few chargers offer specialized modes like “desulfation,” which helps a battery regain its chemical balance through carefully timed charge-and-discharge cycles. A “quick charge” can very rapidly (but safely) prepare a battery for use. A few battery chargers also offer a “jump start mode” that can start a car or motorcycle with a dead battery, but this is rare, and most of the time you’ll need a separate jump starter for that task.

Most chargers in this roundup are designed for conventional lead-acid (flooded cell) or Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) batteries, which you’ll find in newer vehicles. If you have a vehicle with a lithium-ion battery, like some new BMWs, or a customized car with ultra-compact batteries from manufacturers like Braille, you’ll need a charger with that capability—different battery chemistries require specific charging protocols.

If you are dealing with a cramped garage, or travel between storage spaces throughout the seasons, consider a “wall wart” or direct-mount charger. The former keeps all the charging mechanisms in a large plug that some people might compare to model-train transformer plugs. The latter bolts into your car and plugs directly into the wall.

Not anymore. Today's smart chargers, like the ones in our article, won't overcharge a battery or give it more than it can handle. And choosing a more powerful charger won't shorten your battery's lifespan; quite the opposite, in fact!

It's usually as simple as removing the bolt from both battery clamps, slipping the thin copper loops between the bolt and washer, and reinstalling. Then you can coil the quick-disconnect cord in a convenient place, like inside a motorcycle fairing or under a car hood. The cables can melt when exposed to serious heat, so don't let them touch an exhaust pipe.

Yes, if the batteries are in reasonably decent condition. Any charger rated at 2 Amps or more should be able to rotate between multiple vehicles. If you have more than three or four, consider buying multiple chargers.

#6429. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

#6426. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

#6425. Can a Power Station Cut Down Your Electric Bill? Yes, Based on Your Rates and Setup.

Time-of-use mode found in some power stations utilizes an integrated battery backup to reduce the time your appliances spend on the grid when rates are highest.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Can a power station help me save money on my electric bill? I reviewed enough units to know the opportunity is there if the station has a time-of-use mode (TOU, for short). Stations with this feature utilize integrated battery backups to reduce time spent on the grid when rates are highest. That sounds pretty cool, but I’ve often wondered just how much money it can actually save.

I discovered it depends on a number of factors. For your best chance to save the most money, you need to live in an area where variable electric rates are available. You also need to primarily use portable power for a whole-home backup system or on appliances that are always running, like a refrigerator, to get the most out of TOU mode. That’s because the cost of electricity is typically lowest in a variable-rate system when demand is at its lowest, during the middle of the night, for example.

Below is everything I’ve learned about setting up TOU mode on a portable power station and how to find out how much money this feature can save you over time.

Power stations with TOU mode tend to be large or designed for home backup, such as whole-home battery-based systems or models designed to back up one or two appliances, like refrigerators. But some smaller portable power stations offer this mode. Jackery’s HomePower series, including the 1000 Plus v2, for example, offers this mode within its mobile app.

If you’re someone who primarily uses portable power for camping trips and other activities, it’s worth noting that TOU mode may not be very useful to you. To effectively switch back and forth between peak and non-peak hours, the station must be consistently connected to grid power and the devices you want to run from it. It makes more sense to plan a TOU-based setup with a more dedicated type of power station, or a portable one that you don’t plan to move around very often.

First, you need to know if variable rates are available in your region and how they operate. Electrical utilities are not regulated at the federal level in the U.S., so this varies from state to state. Utilities in states that regulate their electric utilities may offer variable rates (sometimes called time-variable pricing), while states that deregulate may have variable-rate options through the various energy providers.

For example, in my home state of Pennsylvania, the primary electric company offers only flat rates. However, Pennsylvania is a deregulated market, so if I opt for a different energy provider, I can select one that offers variable rates. Some states, like Texas, even offer times of the day when rates are free.

In most cases, variable-rate programs require you to sign up in some form or another to activate these rates, so call your local provider to get the details of what is available to you.

Once you have that worked out, setting up your station is fairly straightforward. Choose the device or devices you wish to run partially during the day from battery power and connect them to the power station. Plug the power station into an outlet in the house. From there, everything is set in your power station’s app by selecting the TOU working mode, which can usually be found in the advanced settings.

The app then prompts you to enter the high-rate (peak) hours and the low-rate hours, along with the price for each rate (dollars per kilowatt-hour). This helps the app calculate savings over time, so you don’t have to. Once that is set up, the battery automatically powers your devices during peak hours and returns to the grid during low-rate hours. It also uses the low-rate hours to recharge the battery from the grid, or you can opt to recharge it from a portable solar panel.

If only flat rates are available to you, you could still use TOU mode and choose a set of hours each day to run on battery power; there just won’t be the advantage of opting for cheaper rate times.

The potential for saving money isn’t as simple to figure out. While the apps can generally track savings over time, variable rates can fluctuate (e.g., some utilities change them every few months), so unless you are keeping up with the fluctuation and adjusting the app accordingly, those numbers can be off.

The amount of actual savings is also tricky to predict. Much of it depends on how many devices in your home you plan to run using this mode and how low the rate is during off-peak hours. The latter will have the most effect, and the savings will be harder to realize if you’re only powering one or a few things.

For example, if you’re using Bluetti’s FridgePower to power only a refrigerator in TOU mode, that appliance typically only draws 300 watts on average, so the actual savings by running it from the grid only during off-peak hours might only equate to a few dollars per month, maybe even less. Then again, if you’re powering a lot of stuff in TOU mode using a large-capacity whole-home system, the savings will likely be more significant.

Something else to keep in mind is that the most expensive devices to run in your home are usually the higher-voltage systems such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning (HVAC) and high-voltage appliances such as ovens and electric dryers. These need to be paired with stations that can handle 220/240-volt output (only the larger ones can) and need a significant amount of battery capacity to operate over several hours. This requires a large system with at least one or two additional batteries (if not more), which can cost several thousand dollars. The cost of chasing the savings enabled by the TOU mode could likely take a few years to actually be recouped.

While the money-saving potential can be a bit hard to estimate or feel significant, especially in the short term, this feature will shave something off your monthly bill, so it’s definitely worth looking into, especially if you have a large system that powers several always-on devices.

It might not be a reason to buy a power station for home backup, but it’s certainly a good feature to have at your disposal. It may not be a huge help, but there’s no real downside either.

#6424. Sunflowers reveal a surprising secret about how plants sense light

New research reveals why sunflowers sometimes grow toward weaker light instead of brighter sources, challenging assumptions about plant behavior.

Plants grow toward light, so it seems natural that they would always bend toward whatever shines brightest.

Young sunflowers don’t always follow that rule. When two equally strong lamps shone on them from opposite sides, the seedlings grew toward a third, weaker lamp instead.

The researchers concluded that plants don’t simply grow wherever the most light is.

Different sides of a sunflower stem respond to the light they receive. Those signals combine to guide growth, allowing two equally strong lights from opposite directions to effectively cancel each other out.

Yasmine Meroz, a professor at Tel Aviv University, carried out the study with Ahron Kempinski, Amir Porat, and Mathieu Rivière. All four are part of the university’s Center for Physics and Chemistry of Living Systems.

“What is fascinating is that plants can integrate complex information about their environment without a brain or central processing system,” Meroz said.

“The computation emerges from the way light is sensed and processed locally across the stem.”

The team worked only with sunflower seedlings about a week old, grown and tested indoors under blue lamps. How full-grown plants handle light coming from many directions outdoors hasn’t been tested.

In many animals, sense organs such as skin collect signals and a brain sorts them out. A plant has no brain to do that job.

Instead, the light-sensing proteins that steer its bending are found mainly in the outermost layer of cells on the stem. Each patch of the stem’s surface responds to the light that lands on it.

Some light also passes straight through. Using a 3D-printed sleeve to hold seedling stems in front of a light meter, the team ran 31 measurements.

On average, about 10% of the light hitting a stem got through, giving the sensors on the far side a weak signal pointing the opposite way. A stem bends by growing faster on one side than the other.

The team’s model adds up the light signals from every side to work out which way the stem will grow.

Young sunflowers famously track the sun as it moves across the sky.

The sunflowers in this study were much younger, grown at 77°F (25°C) and picked when they stood 0.4 to 1.2 inches (1 to 3 cm) tall.

The team painted two fluorescent dots near each seedling’s tip under dim green light, so the plants wouldn’t start reacting to light too early.

Strips of blue LEDs then lit five seedlings at a time while the plants were photographed from the side for at least 21 hours.

The angle between the two dots showed how far each tip had bent. After about 16 hours, the seedlings settled at a steady angle.

With one lamp, brighter light made the seedlings bend further. But across a tenfold range of brightness, the bend didn’t keep pace.

The team’s measurements fit a pattern in which a light twice as bright produces a signal well short of twice as strong.

Senses in many species work this way, responding to how much a signal changes compared with where it started.

The researchers compare this response to human hearing, where a 10-decibel increase is typically perceived as roughly twice as loud.

Compression of this kind lets a plant respond across a wide range of light, from shade under other leaves to direct sunlight, the researchers wrote.

Next, the team placed seedlings between two lamps facing each other at different strengths.

The seedlings bent toward the brighter lamp, and a bigger gap in brightness meant a bigger bend, though again not in a straight-line way.

The team’s model, using the compression measured with one lamp, predicted where those seedlings would settle. It matched the measurements well, with one small miss the team put down to slightly uneven lighting.

By the model’s logic, two lamps of equal strength on opposite sides should cancel each other out.

The two-lamp runs already suggested as much, because nearly matched lamps barely moved the seedlings off vertical.

So the team added a third lamp at a right angle to the first two. The two strong lamps were set almost exactly equal, and the third was less than half as bright as either one.

The team filmed 34 seedlings from above for 21 hours, and a computer program trained to recognize leaves tracked where each plant grew.

On average, the seedlings grew almost straight toward the weak lamp, less than 1 degree off, though individual plants varied widely around that average.

The researchers wrote that this result isn’t intuitive for a plant that needs light to make food. In their view, the finding shows that plants don’t grow to collect as much light as possible.

The same math predicts something stranger. With two lamps at a right angle, one brighter than the other, the most light comes from a direction between them, closer to the brighter lamp.

But in the team’s model, the plant compresses each lamp’s signal before adding them up, which changes how strong the two signals are compared with each other.

So the direction the plant favors ends up a little off from the direction of the most light.

The researchers call this a kind of optical illusion, though it doesn’t mean the plant sees anything.

In their calculations, the gap is at most about 6 degrees, and it disappears when the two lamps are equally bright or when only one is on.

“Our work shows how the physical organization of a sensory system can determine how an organism perceives and responds to its environment,” Meroz said.

The team couldn’t measure the illusion in its living seedlings.

Growing sunflower stems trace circling motions, and in the final three hours of the three-lamp test, a seedling’s growth direction typically varied by about 17 degrees.

A 6-degree shift is too small to see against that much motion. The team’s analysis found that the circling wouldn’t average the distortion away.

Meroz’s lab in the university’s School of Plant Sciences and Food Security has studied the same circling in crowded sunflowers before. Here, that motion limited what the experiment could detect.

The model also missed one detail of the movement. Real seedlings bent past their final angle and then eased back, and the simulated ones didn’t.

The team suggested that uneven growth along the stem, or the stem sagging under its own weight, could explain why.

Bacteria and some other single cells also sense their surroundings across their whole surface, with no brain in charge.

“This principle may extend far beyond plants, to cells, bacteria, and other living systems that rely on distributed sensing,” Meroz said.

For now, the optical illusion remains a mathematical prediction. Confirming it will require measurements precise enough to distinguish the subtle effect from the seedlings’ natural circling movements.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

An aerial view of the tomb where archaeologists found the shrine maiden statuette.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.

The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6422. A college student searching rocky glaciers in Yellowstone finally discovered one of the rarest insects in the world

A University of Wyoming student discovered three rare ice crawlers in Yellowstone, marking the first known sightings of these cold-loving insects in Wyoming.

In summer 2026, a college student named Will Anderson found three rare bugs called ice crawlers on rocky glaciers in Yellowstone National Park.

As a student at the University of Wyoming, Anderson had spent the whole previous year looking for them without any luck. Ice crawlers are some of the rarest insects on Earth.

Ice crawlers belong to Grylloblattodea, one of the rarest orders of insects in the world. Only 35 species have been described, and many are known only from single localities.

Anderson is a biology major from Casper and a junior in the Wyoming Research Scholars Program. He works with Audrey Lindsteadt, a third-year Ph.D. student in the university’s Program in Ecology and Evolution.

“I am interested in this insect because there is so much not known about them, with their life history, habitat, and distribution all not being fully understood,” Anderson said.

“I also am passionate about and interested in their alpine habitats, which are understudied,” he added.

Starting in late July 2025, the pair surveyed 14 rock glaciers in the Red Mountains next to Heart Lake, in southwestern Yellowstone. They found no ice crawlers, even though Anderson also checked snowfields and set overnight traps.

Most snowfields had already melted by then. The area also had fewer glaciers than ideal, and most of them were small or inactive.

“Despite the close proximity to their known distribution and the plentiful suitable habitat, Gryllos have never been found in Wyoming,” Lindsteadt explained. “Therefore, Will hypothesized the rock glaciers and nearby snowfields that we are studying could have Gryllos.”

On a cold, snowy six-day backpacking trip in late June and early July 2026, Anderson found two ice crawlers near Antler Peak in northwest Yellowstone. Both turned up under rocks he flipped on a large rock glacier.

In mid-July, a mother grizzly and her two-year-old cub bluff-charged the pair and blocked their planned route.

They scrambled up Grey Peak instead and slid down to its two rock glaciers, where Anderson caught a third one. In August, he searched several alpine glaciers in Grand Teton National Park but came up empty.

Over the summer of 2026, he and Lindsteadt walked about 170 miles (274 kilometers).

“The specimens I collected in Wyoming are so far identified to the species Grylloblatta campodeiformis, which is the most widespread North American species, having populations in Montana, British Columbia, and Alberta,” Anderson noted.

He briefly kept two of the insects alive. He could not tell whether they were feeding on the dead insects and plant matter he gave them.

Ice crawlers are wingless insects that stay active in cold conditions, according to North Carolina State University entomologists. Most species are active below freezing and usually die above 50°F (10°C).

They develop through incomplete metamorphosis, from egg to nymph to adult, and their growth is slow. Some may need up to seven years to complete a single generation.

The University of Wyoming describes them as extremophiles that live at temperatures as low as 21°F (-6°C) in humid alpine settings.

By day, they hide under cool rocks near snow and ice. At night, they scavenge, eating mostly other invertebrates, including insects blown onto the snow, along with some plant material.

Little is known of their diet when they live more permanently under the snow, or in the soil through summer and winter.

The order lives in northeastern Asia, Siberia, the western U.S. and Canada. In North America, small, isolated populations occupy mountains and caves in several western states, British Columbia and Alberta.

Rock glaciers resemble alpine glaciers, but a layer of debris covers their ice, insulating and protecting it.

Lindsteadt suspects that ice crawlers prefer rock glaciers to non-glacial talus fields or snowfields because rock glaciers are colder, more humid and more permanent.

“Obviously, with just three species detections, we cannot confidently identify their habitat preferences,” Lindsteadt said. “But they at least point us in a promising direction.”

Yellowstone holds 58 known rock glaciers, and none had been visited or studied before this project. Next summer, the team plans to survey 17 rock glaciers in eastern Yellowstone and revisit others.

Ice crawlers are generally restricted to high-elevation glaciers or low-elevation caves with permanent ice, according to Purdue University entomologists.

The same entomologists warn that many of these habitats are at risk as glaciers and ice fields recede with climate change.

In Anderson’s view, the insects probably play a small part in these ecosystems because of their rarity, but they still belong to the food chains and nutrient cycles of their extreme habitats.

“More importantly, we can use ice crawlers to better understand how these ecosystems work and be more effective managers of them,” he argued.

He is also working on a paper he hopes to publish in a leading alpine or entomology journal.

Anderson will present the findings at the Entomological Society of America’s 74th annual meeting in Columbus, Ohio, on November 8 to 11.

The information was obtained from the University of Wyoming.

#6421. Ozempic and similar drugs have a surprising benefit that goes beyond weight loss

New research suggests that Ozempic and Wegovy may reduce long-term sick leave, benefiting employers and taxpayers without increasing workers' earnings.

Ozempic is best known for lowering blood sugar and body weight. But does better health also mean more time at work and higher earnings? A study from Denmark found that the answer isn’t so simple.

Adults there who started Ozempic spent less time on long-term sick leave in the years that followed. But they were no more likely to hold a job than similar adults who hadn’t started the drug yet, and their income didn’t rise.

The money saved went to employers and local governments, which pay for sick leave in Denmark, instead of to the patients themselves.

Meltem Daysal of the University of Copenhagen and four colleagues, including economists at the ROCKWOOL Foundation and Duke University, carried out the analysis.

Their paper is an early release that the authors may still revise, and it compares patients in national health and tax records instead of assigning anyone to take the drug.

Ozempic, a brand of the drug semaglutide, became available in Denmark in August 2018.

During the study years, it was approved there for adults whose type 2 diabetes wasn’t under control with diet, exercise and earlier medicines.

The team started with 9,794 Danes who began taking Ozempic in its first 17 months on sale.

Comparing them with people who never took it would mislead, because patients who start a new diabetes drug tend to differ from those who don’t.

So the researchers paired each early starter with someone who began Ozempic four years later. Each pair was matched on age, sex, diabetes and obesity, and then on income, education, marriage and how often they saw a family doctor.

The matching produced 7,011 pairs. Until the later starters began their own treatment, they showed what might have happened to the early starters without the drug.

Everyone was between 30 and 59 at the end of 2017. That way, all of them would still be under 65, and more likely to be working, when the study ended.

In the United States, many patients stop these drugs early. One study of American patients with private insurance found that only 40% to 60% were still taking them after a year.

The Danish patients stuck with it. Four years after their first prescription, 75% of the early starters were still filling prescriptions for semaglutide, and most of those who quit did so in the first year.

Ozempic is subsidized in Denmark, where a month’s supply cost 1,117 Danish kroner, about $212, in 2019. A patient’s yearly out-of-pocket spending on subsidized prescriptions was capped at 4,300 kroner, about $681.

Earlier research has often blamed side effects when patients quit. The authors suggested that what patients pay may also play a big part in whether they stay on the drug for years.

In this study, sick leave counted as long-term once a spell ran past 30 days. Before starting Ozempic, the patients spent about 5.5% of their months on long-term sick leave.

Over the four years after the first prescription, that share fell by about 1 percentage point compared with the later starters, a drop of 17.3%. Put simply, long sick leave became about a sixth less common among the people taking the drug.

In the first two years, the early starters spent about 0.8 percentage points less of their time on long sick leave than the later starters. In years three and four, the gap reached about 1.1 points.

Payments from local governments, which cover sick leave after the first 30 days, fell by 19.4% over the same period.

The authors interpreted the decline as evidence of a treatment effect, noting that sick leave had followed similar patterns in both groups before the early starters began treatment.

The decline appeared in nearly every group the team checked when it split patients by sex, age and education. Women had the largest drop, while the estimates for men and for people under 50 were less certain.

The records can’t show exactly why sick leave fell, but the team found some clues in them.

After starting Ozempic, patients were less likely to visit an emergency department and less likely to fill prescriptions for heart and blood vessel medicines.

Earlier randomized trials, including one from 2016, found that semaglutide lowers the risk of serious heart problems such as heart attacks and strokes in high-risk patients. Events like those often keep a person away from work for weeks.

The authors called that a plausible explanation for the drop in sick leave, not a proven one. Their records include no weight or blood sugar measurements, so the team couldn’t track how each patient’s health changed.

Over the same four years, the team found no change in whether patients had jobs, whether they were in the workforce at all, or how much they earned.

The estimates were precise enough to rule out a rise in employment of more than 0.4 percentage points and a rise in income of more than 0.7%.

The authors traced this to the way Denmark pays for illness.

Employers cover the first 30 days of a worker’s sick leave, and the local government takes over after that. For workers who earn below a cap, those payments can replace all of their usual pay.

So when a worker missed fewer weeks, their income stayed about the same. The savings went to employers and taxpayers.

The team estimated those savings at about 4,163 kroner a year for each employed patient, or 1.3% of a year’s earnings. If shorter sick spells fell by the same share, the total would reach 4,766 kroner, about $722, or 1.5% of earnings.

For Denmark’s budget, this means the drug costs the public less than its pharmacy price suggests. Even so, the authors wrote, the savings remain far smaller than what GLP-1 treatments cost in 2026.

Sick pay in the United States is less generous than in Denmark. There, the authors suggested, similar health gains might show up instead as higher earnings, more hours, or fewer people losing their jobs.

A 2026 study of American women who started GLP-1 drugs to lose weight found large increases in employment among those who hadn’t been working.

The Danish authors wrote that the two studies differ in both their setting and their patients.

The team also checked Wegovy, the semaglutide brand approved in Denmark for weight management.

Among 67,736 new Wegovy users, long-term sick leave fell by about 1 percentage point within the first year, and jobs and income again didn’t rise.

Less than a year of records is too short to judge the long run, and the authors treated the Wegovy job and income results with caution.

Whether the gains last for people who take these drugs mainly to lose weight is still an open question.

Answering it will take longer records of weight-loss patients, ideally from countries where a sick day costs workers more than it does in Denmark.

The study appeared as an IZA Discussion Paper.

#6420. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

This story was updated on October 29, 2026 to include expert input from Emma Stone.
