How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

A chart showing the evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today. The first stars started to appear from the hydrogen fog a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.

These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.

The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.

Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

Carr, C., Cen, R., McCandliss, S., Ford, J., Saldana-Lopez, A., Scarlata, C., Huberty, M. S., Jaskot, A., Flury, S., Oey, M. S., Amorín, R. O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts. Nature Astronomy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02999-z

#6418. Rising temperatures may have a dangerous effect on mental health

New research reveals how extreme heat may increase suicide risk by disrupting sleep and emotional regulation, highlighting a hidden mental health threat.

Extreme heat can do more than exhaust the body. It may also disrupt sleep, weaken emotional control, and increase vulnerability to serious psychological distress.

A new study has identified temperatures at which extreme heat is associated with increased psychological distress, revealing how disrupted sleep and emotional regulation may contribute to suicide risk.

The research was led by scientists from Georgetown University and the World Bank. It draws on a nationally representative panel study of nearly 7,500 adults in Bangladesh.

The researchers found that extreme heat was associated with an increased risk of suicide-related thoughts, with disrupted sleep playing a surprisingly important role.

“Rising global temperatures threaten human mental health on a massive scale,” said lead author Syed Shabab Wahid, an assistant professor of global health at Georgetown.

“In climate-vulnerable nations such as Bangladesh, this heat stress can translate into severe psychological strain and elevated suicide risk.”

The study tracked two interconnected pathways between heat and suicidal cognition: disrupted sleep and emotional dysregulation.

The association between temperature and suicide-related thoughts became statistically significant at 28°C and was strongest at 35°C.

Temperatures this high are common in Bangladesh during the summer months.

At that upper threshold, nearly 30 percent of the total association between heat and suicide risk ran through poor sleep quality alone. Emotional dysregulation accounted for a smaller but still significant 1.8 percent.

Together, poor sleep and difficulties regulating emotions statistically accounted for roughly a third of the observed relationship between heat and suicide-related thoughts.

The study design is worth understanding, because it shaped what the researchers could and couldn’t conclude.

Participants were interviewed twice – once in winter (January–February 2024) and once at the height of summer (May–June 2024).

Suicide risk was measured using the Brief Suicide Cognitions Scale, a validated tool that captures the sense of unbearability, unlovability, and unsolvability that precedes suicidal behavior.

Heat exposure was operationalized as the number of days with maximum temperatures at or above 35°C in the two weeks prior to each interview.

The panel structure meant the same individuals answered both rounds, which allowed the team to compare the same person’s mental state across seasons.

Summer scores were meaningfully worse: average suicide cognition scores rose from 10.99 in winter to 12.96 in summer.

Sleep quality declined. Emotional regulation worsened. Both effects were consistent across age groups, though older adults and women showed the steepest deterioration.

“Imagine a smartphone with a drained battery, overheating processor, and critical apps crashing all at once. Sustained ambient heat acts on the human brain and body in the same way,” Wahid explained.

“The body cannot cool down at night, leading to broken rest and depleting mental reserves. When the emotional processor overheats without restorative recovery, coping mechanisms collapse under stress.”

The study found that risk was notably higher during summer among less educated and poorer populations.

These differences may reflect unequal access to cooling, greater exposure to outdoor heat, and housing conditions that make it harder to escape high temperatures.

Individuals with disabilities showed consistently elevated risk across seasons. Unemployed people reported higher suicide cognition scores than those in most other employment categories.

Urban residents were more susceptible than rural ones. This may reflect the urban heat island effect. Concrete and asphalt absorb and radiate heat in ways that push nighttime temperatures higher.

There’s a global dimension to these findings that goes beyond Bangladesh.

Previous meta-analyses have found that a 1°C increase in monthly mean temperature is associated with a 1.5 to 1.7 percent increase in suicidal outcomes.

Bangladesh sits in a region the IPCC projects will experience some of the worst heatwaves of the coming decades. But the mechanisms the study identified are not unique to South Asia.

“Rather than treating climate-related mental health crises as unpreventable events, public health systems can now focus on intermediate, modifiable targets,” Wahid said. Sleep is one of them.

“Health agencies can monitor heat waves alongside sleep quality disruption indicators to mobilize preventative interventions. Interventions centered on sleep preservation, household cooling access, and community-based emotional regulation training should serve as effective suicide prevention tools during heatwaves.”

The paper points toward green roofing, passive architecture, and low-cost cooling technologies as structural interventions with documented effects on indoor temperatures in Bangladesh.

A pilot study found that buildings with vegetation-covered green roofing maintained temperatures 3.5°C lower than bare rooftops.

Such reductions could help make indoor environments more comfortable during extreme heat, potentially protecting sleep and reducing heat-related stress.

The study has some important limitations.

First, it relies on ambient outdoor temperature rather than indoor measurements. That’s a known proxy problem in Bangladesh, where air conditioning is rare and indoor heat tracks outdoor heat closely.

Humidity data wasn’t available, meaning the full thermal stress experienced by respondents – particularly relevant in a country where wet-bulb temperatures can reach dangerous levels – is likely underestimated.

What the study offers is new evidence that poor sleep and difficulties regulating emotions may help explain the relationship between extreme heat and suicide-related thoughts.

These findings point toward practical ways to reduce the psychological toll of rising temperatures.

Protecting sleep, improving access to cooling, and supporting mental health could become increasingly important as extreme heat becomes more common.

The study is published in the journal Environmental Research.

#6416. China restored its mangrove forests, and something remarkable happened

A 22-year study reveals how China's mangrove restoration efforts transformed coastal habitats and coincided with a dramatic rise in recorded bird diversity.

For decades, China’s coastal mangrove forests were cleared to make room for shrimp farms, ports, and development. By the 1990s, roughly two-thirds of these once-extensive forests had disappeared.

Then China launched an ambitious restoration effort, transforming large stretches of its coastline and creating new opportunities for wildlife to recover.

A study led by Ningbo University tracked what happened next. The researchers used 22 years of satellite imagery across five coastal provinces plus Hong Kong and Macao.

The team analyzed 13,308 Landsat images through Google Earth Engine, and bird survey records were pulled from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility.

The images revealed that the mangrove area grew 166 percent between 1998 and 2020, from around 10,600 hectares to more than 28,000.

Recorded bird species nearly tripled, from 148 to 397. The number of IUCN-threatened species found in these habitats almost doubled.

The sharpest growth came between 2003 and 2008 – 4,558 hectares in five years, the fastest expansion in the study period.

That expansion followed China’s 2000 Wetland Protection Action Plan, which helped direct attention and resources toward coastal habitat recovery. Later environmental protections reinforced those efforts.

Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macao, and Guangxi accounted for more than 88 percent of the national increase. Hainan added 1,678 hectares, while Zhejiang and Fujian – too far north to sustain them reliably – saw modest gains.

The latter occasionally even lost what had been planted, because cold snaps kill seedlings and typhoons don’t negotiate.

In 2008, Typhoon Nuri wiped out 80 percent of newly planted mangrove seedlings in Guangdong in a single pass. This is what restoration in dynamic coastal environments actually looks like up close.

The logic seems simple: plant trees and birds arrive. But the actual mechanism – which the Ningbo team reconstructed using partial least squares path modeling – is much weirder.

Mangrove area had the strongest direct effect on species richness. But the strongest direct driver of overall bird diversity wasn’t the forest itself – it was phytoplankton.

Expanding mangrove forests can influence water chemistry and nutrient flows in adjacent coastal waters.

The researchers found that mangrove expansion was associated with changes in coastal conditions that supported phytoplankton, an important foundation of marine food webs.

These changes may have benefited fish, shrimp, and the birds that feed on them.

Climate, meanwhile, had only indirect effects. It made conditions more suitable for mangrove growth as temperatures rose and rainfall increased.

Average vegetation cover across mangrove stands rose from 31 to 38 percent over the study period.

This suggests the forests were not only expanding but also becoming denser, providing more of the sheltered habitat that birds need for breeding and roosting.

But the researchers also identified an important uncertainty: how much of the apparent increase in bird diversity reflects ecological recovery, and how much comes from improved monitoring?

China’s birdwatching community has exploded over the past two decades, riding rising incomes and platforms like eBird.

Species that were always present but never recorded are now being logged. The jump from 148 to 397 species almost certainly mixes true ecological recovery with improved detection, and there’s no clean statistical way to separate them.

While this acknowledgment doesn’t invalidate the findings – the forest recovery is unambiguous in the satellite data – it should temper any instinct to take the bird numbers at face value.

There’s a second caveat worth noting: mangrove expansion sometimes converts intertidal mudflats, and mudflats are irreplaceable foraging habitat for migratory shorebirds.

Net gain in trees can mean net loss for specific species. Conservation math is rarely as clean as headline percentages suggest.

China’s experience demonstrates that sustained restoration efforts can help reverse decades of mangrove loss.

But it also shows that ecological recovery is complicated, shaped by storms, changing habitats, and the needs of different species.

Restoring coastal ecosystems requires more than planting trees. It requires understanding the entire web of life they support.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

#6415. AI is revealing a hidden world of animal behavior

Artificial intelligence is revealing subtle patterns in animal behavior that scientists have long overlooked, opening new possibilities for research.

For decades, scientists studying mice in laboratory mazes have largely tracked their movements as single dots on video screens.

That dot shows how far the animal went and how fast, but it can’t tell a mouse frozen in fear from one that has fallen asleep or stopped to groom.

Artificial intelligence now lets researchers track the whole body instead, from the curve of the spine to the position of each limb.

A new review of the field finds that this shift has changed what behavior research can measure.

But one of the major obstacles left is something no camera can fix: scientists still don’t share clear definitions for many of the behaviors they study.

The review comes from Ke Chen, Yaning Han, and colleagues. They work at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, two Chinese universities, and a Guangzhou biotech company.

The team’s research summarizes published research rather than reporting new experiments. Most examples involve laboratory mice and rats.

In classic behavior experiments, researchers place an animal in a simple, controlled space and record a handful of numbers.

A Y-shaped maze can test memory by measuring how often a mouse chooses the correct path to food.

In an open-field test, a mouse explores an empty arena. Researchers count how often it ventures into the exposed middle and treat that as a sign of anxiety.

Other setups, such as the Barnes maze, work on the same principle.

Tests like these are easy to standardize. But researchers using them see little of what an animal does on its own. Carrying a mouse from its home cage into an unfamiliar apparatus may also change how it behaves.

The authors described a bigger problem in the gap between these tests and brain research.

Today’s probes can record from thousands of brain cells at once, yet those recordings are often compared against a single number, such as speed or time spent in one zone.

The newer approach uses video, and AI software learns to mark chosen points on the animal’s body in every frame, turning a running mouse into a moving stick figure. Researchers call this pose estimation.

One of the most widely used programs, an open-source tool called DeepLabCut, needs only a modest number of hand-labeled images to get started.

By one estimate cited in a 2021 review, carefully labeling every frame of a one-hour video takes 22 person-hours.

Some labs also add infrared cameras or ultrasonic microphones that pick up calls too high for human ears.

A second layer of software sorts the tracked movements into behaviors. Some programs learn from clips people have already labeled, while others group similar movements without labels.

The label-free approach has turned up movements lasting less than a second that human observers had missed. Still, a pattern a computer can separate isn’t automatically a meaningful behavior, the authors wrote.

Some of the tools the review describes came from teams that included its own authors.

Chen and Kang Huang work for Guangdong BayOne Biotech, which holds patents related to a behavior-analysis technology called BehaviorAtlas. The other three authors reported no financial stake in the company.

Tracking one animal at a time is the simpler job. Once several mice share a space, the software also has to keep track of which mouse is which, and lab mice make that hard.

Many lab mice come from inbred strains or the same litter, so they look nearly identical. Curling up changes a mouse’s outline, and gnawing can leave patches of missing fur.

In the review’s comparison of tracking tools, a program called SLEAP achieved roughly 90% of its maximum tracking accuracy using only about 200 labeled video frames.

Even so, it mixed up the identities of mice about 23 times in every 100,000 video frames, compared with fewer than once for fruit flies.

A single swap matters more than it sounds. If it goes uncorrected, every later measurement for those animals can end up credited to the wrong mouse.

Implanted radio tags tell individuals apart reliably, and farms use the same kind of tag to monitor how much feed and water livestock take in. But implanting a tag is invasive, and the discomfort may change how the animal behaves.

The authors asked how long and how sharply a mouse has to swerve before its path counts as a left or right turn, rather than walking forward.

Without an agreed answer, researchers may rely on their own judgment.

Broader labels are harder. Anxiety-like behavior can mean less time on the open arms of a raised, cross-shaped maze, or a mouse that hugs the walls of an open arena.

Both carry the same name, but the authors wrote that the two tests may capture different things.

Social behavior adds another layer. With two mice, it’s unclear at what distance one counts as approaching the other.

When a third mouse enters the picture, two animals might gang up on one, or one might intervene in a conflict between the others.

In mouse models of Parkinson’s disease, a few points on one forelimb may be enough to spot a tremor.

Researchers running a more detailed study might need to separate normal grasping, shaky grasping and tremor at rest.

Because labs tailor their setups this way, their data often can’t be combined or compared. A shared data format called Neurodata Without Borders is an important first step, the authors wrote, but labs have taken it up unevenly.

The review’s more speculative ideas start with what the authors call “behavioral nucleotides.” In DNA, chemical units called nucleotides line up in sequences that carry genetic information.

The authors suggested describing each sampled moment of movement as a list of numbers and treating it as one candidate unit of behavior.

Strung together by rules they call behavioral syntax, those units would build into larger patterns tied to functions such as foraging or avoiding danger.

If that works, researchers could borrow tools built for analyzing DNA, such as lining up two sequences to compare them.

Researchers might also make short-range forecasts, stated as probabilities, of what an animal will do next.

The idea will only be useful if the units can be defined the same way every time, and chopping smooth movement into steps may lose some gradual changes.

The team also proposed “bilingual robotic animals,” robots that send precise, repeatable signals to live animals. Changing one signal at a time could slowly build a rough dictionary of animal body language.

But a robot can look, move and smell different from a real rat, so an animal may react to its strangeness rather than to the signal.

It’s still an open question whether any of this will help human patients.

Better tracking may make preclinical research, the lab work that comes before testing in people, more precise and easier to repeat.

That promise is limited by species differences, the authors wrote, and by the loose fit between lab tests and human psychiatric conditions.

Computer-generated animals could ease some of the need for live experiments. Virtual mice built from anatomical 3D models can produce training video with the labels already attached.

The National Institutes of Health has also emphasized research methods that reduce animal use.

In one study, software trained on synthetic video estimated poses about as well as software trained on hand-labeled footage.

Other studies measured different things, which makes their numbers hard to compare.

The authors recommended creating shared collections of real-world test videos so researchers can compare how well AI tools perform, whether they were trained on real footage, computer-generated videos or both.

The full study was published in the journal The Innovation Reviews.

#6413. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

#6412. Hubble discovers something strange is missing from nearby galaxies

Hubble reveals a mystery in nearby dwarf galaxies, where powerful stellar explosions appear to have swept away much of their oxygen.

The universe is filled with mysteries, and sometimes the most surprising discoveries involve something that should be there but isn’t.

NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has uncovered one such puzzle in nearby dwarf galaxies.

These small collections of stars appear to be missing enormous amounts of oxygen that should have accumulated over billions of years.

A new study of 37 dwarf galaxies suggests that powerful explosions and stellar winds have been sweeping oxygen out of these galaxies far more efficiently than scientists previously thought.

The findings offer a new perspective on how galaxies evolve and how the chemical ingredients of the universe spread through space.

The spectacular Hubble image above shows NGC 4449, an irregular dwarf galaxy located approximately 12 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Canes Venatici.

Unlike the graceful spiral structure of the Milky Way, NGC 4449 has a chaotic appearance.

Bright blue stars are scattered across its irregular shape, while glowing pink clouds mark regions of active star formation.

These colorful features reveal a galaxy filled with energetic young stars and enormous clouds of gas and dust.

But beneath this dazzling appearance lies a surprising chemical mystery.

NGC 4449 was among the 37 galaxies examined in the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project.

Researchers discovered that dwarf galaxies retain only a small fraction of the oxygen their stars are expected to produce.

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements in the universe. Much of it forms inside massive stars through nuclear reactions.

When these stars reach the end of their lives, many explode as supernovae, releasing oxygen and other elements into their surroundings.

Over time, these materials help enrich the gas from which future generations of stars and planets form.

Scientists expected to find more of this oxygen remaining inside dwarf galaxies. Instead, the new observations suggest that much of it has escaped.

“Oxygen is produced by stars, which are inside of galaxies,” explained Grace Telford, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at the University of Utah.

Because dwarf galaxies have relatively weak gravitational fields, they struggle to hold onto gas propelled outward by powerful stellar winds and supernova explosions.

The study suggests that these winds are even more effective at removing oxygen than existing computer models predict.

The research team used archival observations from Hubble to examine individual stars and reconstruct the galaxies’ histories of star formation.

They combined these observations with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope and ground-based radio telescopes.

By examining oxygen associated with stars, gas, and dust, the researchers could estimate how much oxygen the galaxies had produced and how much remained.

The missing material may be drifting through the diffuse gas surrounding the galaxies or may have escaped farther into intergalactic space.

Exactly where most of it ended up remains uncertain.

The findings are important because oxygen serves as a useful marker for other heavy elements created by stars.

Understanding where these elements travel helps astronomers explain how galaxies develop and enrich their surroundings.

The discovery raises new questions about how small galaxies influence the wider universe.

If dwarf galaxies regularly expel large amounts of oxygen and other elements, they may help distribute materials throughout the universe.

These materials could eventually form new stars and planetary systems.

Kristen Wingfield McQuinn is the GLOW project’s principal investigator and an associate professor at Rutgers University.

“It also helps us learn where and how much galaxies are enriching the space between galaxies, called the intergalactic medium,” said McQuinn.

Researchers hope to investigate even smaller galaxies using NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, followed by detailed observations from Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope.

For now, NGC 4449 offers a striking reminder that galaxies are not isolated collections of stars.

They constantly exchange matter with the space around them, shaping the chemical history of the universe.

The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal.

Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer.

Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same?

Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts.

The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA, this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun.

This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere.

This means that summers between the Northern and Southern hemispheres sit six months out of sync with each other — with Northern summers spanning late June to late September and Southern ones going from late December to late March. (Summers are also defined meteorologically, or relative to changes in weather phenomena, as being the hottest months of the year. Under this definition, Northern summers run from June to August, and Southern ones go from December to February.)

Another difference between Northern and Southern summers is their duration. According to NASA, Northern Hemisphere summers are, on average, 4.5 days longer than Southern Hemisphere summers. (This is with respect to the astronomical definition; meteorologically, Northern summers are longer than Southern ones by two days in non-leap years, but this is due to February being the calendar's shortest month.)

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The 4.5-day difference occurs because Earth's orbit around the sun is slightly elliptical instead of perfectly circular, according to NASA. Consequently, Earth's orbital velocity (the speed at which our planet hurtles around the sun) isn't constant.

Earth isn't the only planet that experiences such a dichotomy in the duration of seasons. According to NASA, Mars does too: Northern summers on the Red Planet are 24 Martian days — 24.66 Earth days — longer than the planet's Southern Hemisphere's summers. This greater difference is because Mars's orbit is much more oval-shaped than Earth's.

During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, Earth is farther away from the sun and thus moving more slowly, said Georg Feulner, a senior researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. This is due to Kepler's second law of planetary motion, he added.

This means that at aphelion ‪(the point at which our planet is farthest from the sun)‬ Earth is traveling at 18.2 miles per second (29.3 kilometers per second). This jumps to 18.82 miles per second (30.29 km/s) at perihelion ‪(the point when Earth is closest to the sun ) which occurs during Southern summers.

While this may seem like a tiny difference in speed, it causes our planet's path around the sun to be 53,686 miles (86,400 kilometers) shorter in a 24-hour-interval at aphelion compared with at perihelion. In other words, Earth covers more "ground" at aphelion than at perihelion over a 24-hour-interval. "Therefore, the time between the Northern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes is longer than the time between the Southern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes, Feulner told Live Science in an email.

A third point of difference is that Northern summers are typically hotter than Southern ones. A 2015 study in the journal Climate Dynamics showed the precise value of this depends on whether temperatures are measured on the surface air, land or ocean, and the latitude at which they're taken. Nonetheless, when averaged over all domains and latitudes, Northern summers are 7.83 degrees Fahrenheit (4.35 degrees Celsius) hotter than Southern ones.

So what's behind this? Earth's changing distance from the sun isn't important. If it were, Earth's aphelion crossing during Northern summers should make them cooler than Southern summers during the perihelion crossing. Instead, several other factors are responsible.

One is the Northern Hemisphere's bigger fraction of land compared to its large water bodies like oceans. "Land has a lower heat capacity than water and so increases temperature more for a given heating than water does," Richard Seager, a professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, told Live Science in an email. As a result, the many inland sites in the Northern Hemisphere heat up rapidly and have higher summer temperatures, according to the UCAR Center for Science Education.

Additionally, Seager said, another difference lies in the way heat is distributed through air and water. The solar heat that land receives warms only the first few feet of the atmosphere, while the heat water absorbs gets mixed throughout its depths. This makes the Southern Hemisphere — with its larger fraction of water — cooler over summer.

The second factor for the North Hemisphere's higher summer temperatures are cross-equatorial ocean currents. Such currents cross the equator, transferring water and heat between the hemispheres. The primary current is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). "The AMOC transports heat from the SH [Southern Hemisphere] to the NH in the Atlantic," Feulner said. This warms Northern oceans and seas, which, in turn, heats up adjacent land-masses.

So, Northern Hemisphere summers are longer and hotter than Southern ones. If you want to stretch out your summer, you now know where to go.

#6410. 12 Years Ago, This Jumbo Jet Vanished Without a Trace. New High-Tech Ocean Robots May Finally Reveal What Happened.

The 2014 disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 remains one of aviation’s greatest unsolved mysteries. Inside the latest high-stakes search to find the missing Boeing 777.

On January 2, 2018, from the port city of Durban in eastern South Africa, a ship departed at dusk. This was no vessel outfitted for a nighttime pleasure cruise. In fact, it looked downright strange. Its hull was a shade of prison-jumpsuit orange. Its bow was adorned with a large, flat platform resembling a helipad. Antennas, some pointy, some contained in two white domes, covered its superstructure. A crane was mounted on the ship’s stern. Belowdecks sat eight autonomous submersibles, each weighing about 4,000 pounds, or the equivalent of a Ford F-150. This ship was heading east, bound for a section of the southern Indian Ocean about 1,500 miles west of Australia. Its mission? To find the notorious Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

When MH370 took off from Kuala Lumpur on March 8, 2014, shortly before 1 a.m. local time, there was no indication it wouldn’t be a routine flight. But the Boeing 777-200ER never reached its destination, Beijing. Instead, after 39 minutes in the air, the jetliner disappeared from radar; about seven hours after that, it vanished altogether. Satellite communications analyzed afterward showed that MH370 had turned southward and continued on that course until it presumably exhausted its fuel supply and crashed in the Indian Ocean off the western seaboard of Australia.

An expansive search was quickly mounted, the largest ever for a missing plane. Some 60 ships and 50 aircraft from 26 countries participated, at a cost of more than $150 million. More than 46,000 square miles of Indian Ocean seabed were scanned over a three-year period.

But the plane was never located, and the question of MH370’s whereabouts set off a freneticism rivaled perhaps only by the mystery of Amelia Earhart’s fate on her final flight. In the decade-plus since the plane vanished, numerous and varied hypotheses have surfaced. The aircraft crashed somewhere else, some suggested. Others insisted the plane was shot out of the sky. So vexing was MH370’s disappearance that it even spawned a Netflix docuseries in 2023. Still others contend that, without a doubt, MH370 is on the bottom of the southern Indian Ocean.

Which explains the odd-looking ship that set off on its easterly course in 2018. The craft, a Norwegian-built research vessel named Seabed Constructor, was leased to Ocean Infinity, a deep-sea exploration firm with offices in Europe, Canada, Australia, and the United States. The Malaysian government contracted the company on a no-find, no-fee basis to look for MH370—a mission that promised a reward of up to $70 million. Over several months, Ocean Infinity used its autonomous subs to scan a grid of 9,600 square miles just north of the location where the original underwater search took place. By May of that year, having found nothing, the company suspended its mission.

Bringing the story of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 to a definitive close has been equal parts confounding and elusive. A fool’s errand, one might say. But in spring 2025, the government of Malaysia again contracted the firm—now equipped with new vessels of its own design, as well as advanced underwater robots—to mount a fresh search for MH370. In taking up the search again, in one of the toughest marine environments in the world, Ocean Infinity would be risking money and its reputation in the process. What if, for the second time, it failed to find a debris field of MH370 under the waters of the southern Indian Ocean? What if the black boxes couldn’t be located? What if we never get a definitive answer to how Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 went missing without a trace?

After its 12:42 a.m. takeoff from Kuala Lumpur, with 227 passengers and 10 flight attendants on board, Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 quickly reached its cruising altitude of 35,000 feet and steered toward Beijing. Flying the plane were first officer Fariq Abdul Hamid, 27, and pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah, 53. For Hamid, this was his final training flight before becoming a fully certified pilot. He was in good hands. Zaharie (who was known by his first name) was one of the most senior captains at Malaysia Airlines. He also owned a sophisticated Microsoft flight simulator that he used frequently at home.

At 1:08 a.m., MH370 flew out over the Malaysian coastline, soaring above the South China Sea toward Vietnam. Just 11 minutes later, when the handoff from Kuala Lumpur controllers to Vietnam’s air traffic jurisdiction was about to take place, air traffic control in Kuala Lumpur radioed MH370 one final time.

“Malaysian three-seven-zero, contact Ho Chi Minh one-two-zero-decimal-nine. Good night,” they said.

“Good night. Malaysian three-seven-zero,” came the reply from the cockpit.

Those were the last words ever heard from the plane.

Soon the Vietnamese controllers saw MH370 cross into its airspace. But then something unexpected happened. Air traffic relies on secondary radar, whereby a transponder on an airplane sends a signal that contains information identifying the plane and its cruising altitude. This flight, instead, disappeared entirely from air traffic radar at 1:21 a.m. It wasn’t until four hours later, at around 5:30 a.m., that any sort of emergency response commenced.

The simple fact was that at 6:30 a.m. on March 8, MH370—carrying passengers from China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Australia, New Zealand, France, Canada, the U.S., Ukraine, Russia, Iran, and the Netherlands—should have landed in Beijing. It didn’t.

Making sense of how an object as large as a Boeing 777 goes poof in the night is hard to fathom in our modern age. And for the human mind, which craves order and explanation, it is downright maddening—which might explain the bevy of individuals, with no connection to the flight whatsoever, who jumped in eager to provide answers. Over the many years since MH370’s disappearance, a variety of theories emerged about what happened to the plane. One scenario involves MH370 traveling toward Diego Garcia, a small atoll in the Indian Ocean where the U.S. has an army base, before being shot down. Another scenario claims the plane landed in the jungles of Cambodia. Other theories as to what happened to the flight received major airtime in 2023 during Netflix’s three-part docuseries MH370: The Plane That Disappeared. The plane, one person speculated, was hijacked by Russian agents and rerouted to Kazakhstan. Another person claimed the U.S. Air Force shot down MH370 over the South China Sea.

Whether the U.S. Air Force was really responsible was never seriously considered by Malaysia. But officials had suspected that the plane crashed in the South China Sea en route to Beijing. Accident investigators from Europe, Australia, and the U.S. teamed up with the Malaysian government and began searching the sea’s surface for any floating debris. That search was called off in April 2014 when nothing was found.

Yet within a week after MH370 apparently flew off the map, another theory surfaced in the Wall Street Journal. The article contains, to this day, the most plausible and reasonable explanation, one agreed upon by experts in aviation, satellite communications, and government: MH370 continued flying for hours after it disappeared from radar, turned west, away from its expected destination in Beijing, and then southward, ultimately meeting its demise in the waters of the southern Indian Ocean.

After the article was published, the Malaysian government eventually admitted that the account was true—which meant it had carried on a pointless search in the South China Sea for weeks. (In a comprehensive article for The Atlantic written in 2019, the late author and pilot William Langewiesche noted that autocratic bureaucracies with government-owned airlines generally want bad press to go away. It would be better, in other words, not to solve the puzzle, but to make the matter fade into memory as quickly as possible.)

To arrive at such a conclusion, the WSJ relied on an analysis of technical data from Inmarsat, a company that provides satellite services on land, at sea, and in the air. Although MH370 disappeared from air traffic radar screens, a feat easily achieved by whomever was manning the cockpit controls, it continued to link up every so often to a geostationary Inmarsat satellite over the Indian Ocean. Called “handshakes,” these linkups are electronic blips that, while tiny, yielded the most information about what happened to the plane. There were seven handshakes altogether: two that came automatically from the plane, and five others initiated automatically from an Inmarsat ground station in Perth, Australia.

The Inmarsat linkups provided two critical values. The first value is the burst timing offset, or BTO. It’s a measure of the round-trip time it takes for a blip to go from a ground station to a satellite to (in this case) an aircraft, then back up to the satellite and back to the ground station. It’s essentially the distance between the plane and the satellite, and that information gets processed as a series of rings, or arcs, of all possible locations. When it comes to MH370, the most important arc is the last one, the seventh, which the plane crossed at 8:19 a.m. Kuala Lumpur time. What’s important to note is that the seventh arc contains two location possibilities: If MH370 turned north, it may have ended up in Kazakhstan. If it went south, its location is in the southern Indian Ocean.

Determining the direction comes down to the second value: burst frequency offset, or BFO. It shows the difference between the expected frequency from a transmitter and the frequency ultimately received. As Langewiesche explained, the BFO is “a measure of radio-frequency Doppler shifts associated with high-speed movement in relation to satellite position.” Think about it and it makes sense: Neither planes nor satellites are stationary objects, so expected signals won’t match signals that actually get transmitted between the two. (That’s the Doppler effect, that change in frequency of radio waves.) Measuring BFO is a way to determine a plane’s speed and heading. During their investigation into the satellite data, Inmarsat technicians in London picked up on a distortion in the BFO value that suggested MH370 turned south at 2:40 a.m. Further analysis showed that MH370 entered a steep descent, as much as 15,000 feet per minute, just before crossing the seventh arc, which presumably happened after the plane ran out of fuel and both of its engines failed. From there it would have plunged violently into the ocean and shattered into millions of confetti-like pieces, to use Langewiesche’s analogy.

And it’s the satellite data, too, that paints a picture of MH370’s deviated flight path. Once the plane disappeared from secondary radar, it did an about-face over the South China Sea, flew back across Malaysia, over the Strait of Malacca separating Malaysia to the northeast and Indonesia to the southwest, and then, very suddenly, made a sharp turn to the southwest, away from the Andaman Sea to the west of Thailand. Accident investigators later determined that this turn was so tight there was no way the plane was still operating on autopilot. Someone was actively steering it.

What the satellite data doesn’t explain is why this happened—or who might have been flying the plane. Was it a potential hijacker? The available evidence says no: Malaysian and Chinese investigators, aided by American FBI agents, ran background checks on all passengers and flight attendants and cleared them of suspicion.

That left the pilots. Fariq Abdul Hamid was a young man with a fresh career as a prestigious Malaysia Airlines pilot ahead of him. Meanwhile, pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah was portrayed in official reports as “someone beyond reproach.” Just a simple family man. Yet as Langewiesche discovered during his reporting in Malaysia, the official depiction of Zaharie did not align with the man’s private life: His wife had moved out, and he was “often lonely and sad.” He admitted to his own friends that he spent his off-hours “pacing empty rooms waiting for the days between flights to go by.” Among aviation investigators, there was strong suspicion, Langewiesche wrote, that Zaharie was clinically depressed.

And then there’s his flight simulator. Most times, Zaharie let simulated flights play out, from wheels up to wheels down. But a forensic investigation of his simulator showed that Zaharie had done a dry run of a flight profile that eerily mirrored MH370’s final flight path. What’s more, Langewiesche reported, “he advanced the flight manually in multiple stages, repeatedly jumping the flight forward and subtracting the fuel as necessary until it was gone.”

Was it Zaharie? One of the pilot’s lifelong friends, another Boeing 777 captain, told Langewiesche he believed it could have been. It’s not like such an event is without precedent: In 1999, for example, the copilot of EgyptAir Flight 990 intentionally crashed the plane into the ocean just south of Nantucket, Massachusetts. In 2015, the copilot of a Germanwings airliner deliberately crashed that plane into the French Alps. In a report published in 2014, the Federal Aviation Administration cites eight different examples of pilot suicides. And surveys conducted of pilots show that 4 percent have thought about taking their own lives.

As the search pressed on over the years, a group of researchers called the Independent Group emerged, made up of engineers and satellite experts who had found one another online as they simultaneously researched the MH370 crash. One of them, an engineer from Virginia named Victor Iannello, was the person who analyzed Zaharie’s simulated flight, coming to the conclusion that the simulation wasn’t some random event, but rather a potentially pivotal clue as to what happened on MH370’s final flight.

“Until MH370 is found and the reason for its disappearance is known, we will be bombarded with conspiracy theories, false leads, books, and movies which will provide nothing but conjecture,” said Prahlad Shirsath three months after the crash. His wife, Kranti, had been on board. “We need to find the truth,” he continued, “and ensure this never happens again.”

Where is that truth? Perhaps at the bottom of the Indian Ocean, the suspected location of the flight’s data recorder and cockpit voice recorder. Recovering the black boxes might help investigators resolve what happened to MH370. But we have to find them first.

The ocean is vast, and the ocean is scary. The deep ocean especially. Consider, for a moment, the possibility that we know more about Earth’s immediate orbit than we know about its oceans. In space, more than 9,000 satellites roam. On Earth, barely one-quarter of the planet’s oceans are mapped in any coherent way so as to make them discernible for underwater exploration.

In May 2014, the governments of Malaysia and China agreed that the Australians should lead the search for MH370, under the auspices of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau. Fugro, a Dutch firm, was contracted to do the work, with payment coming from Malaysia, China, and Australia. Given the satellite data that suggested splashdown on or about the seventh arc, an area of roughly 11,500 square miles across the arc was selected for exploration. This put the search area between 930 and 1,700 miles away from Australia’s western coast.

“Unforgivable” is perhaps the best word for describing the conditions of the Indian Ocean where search efforts were concentrated. The area saw ripping winds as high as 50 miles an hour, sudden powerful storms marked by 30-foot-high swells, and dense rain and fog. These were the least ideal conditions for sending ships out to sea for long periods of time, far from the closest ports, in a search for the maritime equivalent of a needle in a haystack.

When the underwater search for the remains of MH370 finally kicked off, the depths of the southern Indian Ocean were a mystery. An impressive level of surveying was conducted between May and December of 2014—with further mapping through early 2017—to even understand the topography of the deep ocean floor in this part of the world. It had never been mapped before. Fugro deployed three ships: the Equator, equipped with a hull-mounted echo sounder (to measure depth); the Discovery, with side-scan sonar; and the Supporter, which deployed a single autonomous underwater vehicle with side scanners, sonar, and an echo sounder. In all, close to 275,000 square miles of the deep ocean was surveyed, an area much larger than the search zone but valuable nonetheless for understanding the terrain.

Ridges, peaks, valleys, even underwater volcanoes covered the seabed. Most concerning was a deep underwater canyon that sliced horizontally through the seventh arc, believed by some to be the area where the remains of MH370 would be found. Dubbed Broken Ridge, it was formed by tectonic plate shifts more than 40 million years ago. Its depths reached between 2,000 and 20,000 feet beneath the ocean’s surface; sections of its topography were covered in sediment as thick as 1,000 feet.

“It’s like trying to imagine the Rocky Mountains underwater,” says Mike Exner, another member of the Independent Group. Exner is a retired entrepreneur from Colorado with a background in electrical engineering and satellite communications, having founded several of his own companies. He has also been a licensed pilot for more than 50 years. Exner was the person who studied Inmarsat data and civilian radar—primary radar scans resulting from simple pings about objects in the sky—to conclude that in MH370’s final hours, a flight to the seventh arc would not have been possible if there had been some sort of computer glitch or other systems failure.

“All those turns had to be done manually,” Exner says. “I think we’re about 99 percent sure Zaharie did it.” He adds that he can’t be 100 percent sure but says that once you consider the backgrounds of his copilot, the cabin crew, and the passengers, many of the signs point to him.

For almost three years, Fugro’s ships looked across areas on or near the seventh arc for any signs of the plane. Admittedly, there was a technological element working against them. Autonomous underwater vehicles have been game changers in underwater search and rescue, but they still come with certain drawbacks. Traditional radio waves with meaningful data rates don’t penetrate seawater at even paltry depths of six inches. Communication from ship or shore to a vehicle relies instead on sound waves. But even those become useless once the vehicle is roughly five miles away from its launch point.

“You have more contact with the Mars rover than you do [with] . . . a deep survey vehicle,” says J. Carl Hartsfield, director and senior program manager of the Oceanographic Systems Lab at the nonprofit Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts.

So we humans have to place a great deal of trust in technology that we can’t control once it gets out into the ocean. What’s more, Fugro had only one autonomous underwater vehicle at its disposal, and its maximum diving depth was 13,000 feet, which meant it wasn’t reaching the seabed most of the time. As the years went on, the search zone was expanded from the original 23,000 square miles to an area surpassing 46,000 square miles. But not a scrap of the plane was found, and on January 17, 2017, the Australian-led search was suspended, pending further evidence of the plane’s location.

Could it be that MH370 really isn’t near the seventh arc? Could it have ended up somewhere else? David Mearns, a marine scientist who has led several deep-ocean explorations, says there are only two ways to explain why any piece of the aircraft wasn’t found underwater.

“One, they haven’t looked in the right place. Or two, they’ve looked in the right place, but they missed it,” he says. “Anybody who comes up with anything else doesn’t know what they’re talking about.”

By the time Ocean Infinity arrived at the scene of the crash in January 2018, much more had been deduced about MH370’s probable location. While the initial underwater search took place, an amateur campaign to search for debris from the missing plane began. At the center of this was Blaine Gibson, a Seattle-based lawyer with a penchant for wearing a fedora. (The connection to Indiana Jones isn’t lost on him. By his own admission, Gibson is fascinated by mysteries and archaeology. According to him, he once went searching for the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-plated chest containing the tablets on which the Ten Commandments were inscribed.)

“I was astonished to learn that there was no organized search of beaches and shorelines,” he says. “It always seemed to me that the first piece of debris from this plane was probably just going to be found washed to shore by someone walking on the beach.”

He was right. In July 2015, a flaperon, an airfoil that attaches to a plane wing next to the flap, was discovered by a beach cleaning crew on the French island of Réunion, more than 3,500 miles west of Australia. A right wing flap was found on Pemba Island off the coast of Tanzania, in East Africa, in June 2016. And about four months earlier that same year, Gibson located a honeycomb object broken off from a plane’s horizontal stabilizer with the words “No Step” written on it, a piece that was confirmed to be “almost certainly from MH370 by matching part number, stencil, paint, and composition,” says Gibson. In all, more than 50 pieces of debris have been found so far, much of it on Africa’s eastern coast. (The currents in the Southern Hemisphere move in a counterclockwise swirl: east to west when they’re close to the equator; the opposite direction farther south.)

The significance of the physical evidence can’t be overstated. It appears to confirm that the plane crashed in the southern Indian Ocean, that it shattered on impact, and that there should still be more debris left on the ocean floor. The discoveries also refined the search area: Drift analysis conducted by the University of Western Australia put the crash site at a latitude somewhere between 28.3 degrees south and 33.2 degrees south.

In other words, the evidence provided Ocean Infinity a tighter target. In 2018, Seabed Constructor started its search grid at about 35 degrees south and some 1,300 miles to the southwest of Australia’s west coast. It was also better equipped this time, having brought eight autonomous free-swimming submersibles called HUGINs. These robot crafts, designed and manufactured by Norway-based Kongsberg Discovery, are able to reach depths of 20,000 feet. Each comes with a lithium-polymer battery pack weighing 660 pounds; that allows for around 60 hours of uninterrupted search time. Each is also equipped with a downward-pointing sonar system as well as side-mounted sonars to send out pings to objects on the ocean floor. Onboard magnetometers on every HUGIN can confirm whether a return ping indicates something metallic in nature.

Back in January 2018, The Economist reported that Seabed Constructor was “the most advanced civilian survey vessel,” and predicted that if it couldn’t find MH370, it was “likely that nothing will, and that the mystery of MH370 will remain unsolved.” In May, Ocean Infinity turned back to port, having found nothing on the ocean floor.

That two underwater searches proved fruitless has led to differing views as to where, exactly, the plane landed in the southern Indian Ocean. Richard Godfrey, a retired British aerospace engineer and a founding member of the Independent Group, believes the plane is farther north on the seventh arc. His conclusion largely rests on an analysis he’s conducted of data from WSPR, or Weak Signal Propagation Reporter. Amateur radio operators constantly send test signals and record the data that comes back. Godfrey says that when an aircraft flies through such a signal, it creates a disruption that can be used to track that craft. His results put MH370 inside an 18-mile circle at 29.128 degrees south latitude, approximately 970 miles west of Perth.

“It will only take one more search of this area,” Godfrey told the BBC in 2024, “and we will find MH370.”

Meanwhile, other research groups think differently. One contends MH370 is farther east of the seventh arc, in a 20,000-foot-deep hole that lies along the longitudinal line of Penang Island just off Malaysia’s western coast. Two separate groups believe that MH370 did not dive into the ocean and shatter; they think MH370 came to a controlled, guided landing, and then sank. Part of their argument rests on anomalies in the BFO data, those radio-frequency Doppler shifts. The predicted BFO came in at a much higher frequency than what was observed, possibly indicating that initial thoughts of where the aircraft came to rest are wrong.

One of those pushing this interpretation is Vincent Lyne, a former researcher at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania. He laid out his argument in a paper published in December 2024 and called special attention to the two large-scale searches along the seventh arc.

“A significant positive outcome for ocean research was the huge volume of seafloor data collected across [about 46,000 square miles],” he wrote. “It still remains the most intensely mapped seafloor area of our planet. MH370 was simply not there!”

How these interpretations factored into Ocean Infinity’s new search was unclear. The company is tight-lipped and declined an interview for this article, but CEO Oliver Plunkett did acknowledge Godfrey’s WSPR research in a 2022 teleconference with relatives who lost people on Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

If there’s a new dispute over the fate of MH370, it rests largely on where the plane will be found in the southern Indian Ocean, and not that the plane is somewhere under the seas in that part of the world. Gibson, who discovered part of the plane’s horizontal stabilizer, maintains that there’s no way a controlled landing took place. He cites the more than 50 pieces of debris that have been recovered since MH370 went down. “It’s not intact under water,” he tells me.

Exner, for his part, thinks the WSPR data is no substitute for the Inmarsat satellite communications. “Focus strictly on the seventh arc between 32 and 36 degrees south latitude,” he says. “[MH370 is] probably within 50 miles of that arc. Even though [Ocean Infinity] didn’t find it in the first search, that doesn’t mean it isn’t there.”

When Ocean Infinity ultimately resumed its quest for MH370, it was going back with even newer technology. In the time since its 2018 search, the company had built a fleet of more than 15 ships, ranging from vessels as short as 46 feet and as long as 282 feet. While small crews could climb aboard these ships, all of the vessels were nonetheless designed for remote operation from Ocean Infinity’s control centers at company locations. Ocean Infinity had also developed a line of proprietary underwater autonomous vehicles and acquired additional HUGIN submersibles to aid in its efforts.

The company had also accrued a solid track record of successful searches. Just under six months after Ocean Infinity suspended its search for MH370 in 2018, it discovered the lost Argentine Navy submarine San Juan in the Atlantic Ocean. The following year, it located the remains of the South Korean supertanker Stellar Daisy, which sank in the South Atlantic in 2017. In 2024, Ocean Infinity discovered the wreck of a U.S. World War II destroyer, USS Stewart, that the U.S. Navy had sunk deliberately for target practice in the waters of the Pacific Ocean off San Francisco.

Despite all that, Ocean Infinity trawled the unforgiving waters of the southern Indian Ocean for a few days in March 2025 until rough seas forced it back to port. It resumed searching in late December 2025 and kept at it through January 23, 2026, before departing the search area empty-handed.

“The scale of the challenge both geographically and technologically is almost impossible to comprehend,” said Ocean Infinity’s Plunkett in a March 2026 press release. “If nothing else, we can say with confidence that it isn’t where we looked. That matters—it brings clarity, and it will help those continuing to study the evidence refine their thinking and shape future search strategies.”

Underwater searches, obviously, are not easy or cheap endeavors. When Air France Flight 447 bound for Paris from Rio de Janeiro crashed and sank in the Atlantic Ocean off the northeastern coast of Brazil in 2009, the search team that was dispatched knew where to look for the Airbus jet. And despite it resting at a depth of only about 13,000 feet, the searchers still took almost two years to find it.

Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution’s Hartsfield, whose lab helped facilitate that search, can’t remember the exact figures but estimates that the ships deployed in the search operate at a cost of around $65,000 a day. The Remus 6000 Autonomous Underwater Vehicle used to locate the Airbus cost about another $15,000 a day (in 2026 dollars).

“Although this phase of the search has concluded, our commitment has not,” said Plunkett. “We’re continuing to work with the Malaysian government in the hope of being able to return when circumstances allow.” Ocean Infinity’s current contract runs until June 2026, which means if it hasn’t happened, it’s unlikely that a new search will get underway this year.

But as technology continues to advance, maybe someday an armada of vessels will hit the rough seas near the seventh arc once again—probing the depths, scanning the seabed, sending sonar scans into the darkness—and unearth the newest blips of hope in this maddening unsolved mystery.

Andrew Zaleski, a writer based near Washington, D.C., covers science, technology, and business.

#6409. Carbon removal could reverse economic damage, but some countries would benefit more than others

Removing carbon dioxide could help economies recover from warming, but models suggest richer countries would benefit the most.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere could help reverse some economic damage caused by global warming.

But a new modeling study suggests that richer countries would gain the most, while many places would still face losses left over from warming.

Many climate assessments already count on carbon removal to help meet the Paris Agreement targets. This study asks what a cooler climate might mean for economies around the world.

Wenting Hu of the Institute of Atmospheric Physics, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, led the work with Wenguan Wang of Zhejiang University.

Their team combined climate simulations with an AI model of the world economy.

The model estimated that removal would boost output in almost every region, but only Asia and Europe would recover at least as much as they lost during warming.

The researchers stress that their simplified scenarios do not directly predict any economy’s future.

Earlier research has linked economic growth in states and provinces to daily changes in temperature and rainfall, including extreme weather.

Some methods describe those links with straight lines or simple curves, which the authors say may miss much of the complexity.

Studies of carbon removal have also tended to focus on the cost of removing the gas. Less attention has gone to what economies might gain from a cooler climate.

To explore that question, the team built EconClimNet, a deep learning model. This type of AI learns patterns from large amounts of data.

The researchers gathered economic records from 1,554 states, provinces, and similar regions across 77 countries.

They matched those records with 111 local weather measures from 1979 to 2016, including the number of wet days each year.

The model also accounts for national borders. It connects regions within the same country more closely because their economies tend to rise and fall together.

The team trained it on data from 1979 to 2008, then tested it on unfamiliar data from 2014 to 2016.

For total economic output, it scored 0.77 on a scale where one means a perfect match, compared with 0.59 for the next-best AI method.

The researchers then used six climate models from CMIP6, an international project that compares models using shared experiments. Each simulation began with carbon dioxide at its 1850 level.

The gas increased by 1% a year until it reached four times that level, then followed the same path in reverse. Each phase lasted 140 years.

Temperature and rainfall changes peaked about 20 years after carbon dioxide did. Even when the gas returned to its starting level, the planet stayed warmer and wetter, with smaller temperature swings from day to day.

The researchers measured how closely four weather features returned to their earlier state: average temperature, daily temperature swings, the number of wet days, and the heaviest two-day rainfall.

A recovery score of 100% meant a full return.

Across most of the globe, all four scored above 80%. Daily temperature swings recovered best, while average temperature and wet days recovered less fully on nearly every continent.

Northern North America and central Eurasia showed poorer recovery in average temperature and remained warmer. In these simulations, removing carbon dioxide did not return the climate fully to its earlier state.

When the team fed these climates into EconClimNet, global economic output generally fell as carbon dioxide rose.

Output improved in almost every region once removal began, and rainfall measures ranked among the weather factors the model relied on most.

Oceania had the steepest losses during warming, with a median decline in output of about $1.53 million a year. It also had the largest gains during removal, about $1.41 million a year, but those gains did not cover its earlier losses.

Asia gained about $1.23 million a year during removal, more than the $1.13 million a year it lost during warming. Europe roughly broke even, with gains and losses of about $1.22 million a year.

Every other continent recovered less than it had lost. These figures describe trends in the model, rather than forecasts for real economies.

The team divided countries into richer and poorer halves using economic output per person. Both groups lost output as carbon dioxide rose.

Richer countries saw larger losses, with a median decline of about $1.57 million a year, and every sector shrank. In poorer countries, manufacturing grew slightly, but losses in farming and services outweighed that growth.

The authors suggested that manufacturing in poorer countries may cope better with extreme conditions.

When carbon dioxide fell, both groups improved, with richer countries gaining more: about $1.56 million a year at the median.

Services, including retail, banking, and tourism, gained the most during removal. The longest stretch of wet days in a row was the weather measure that mattered most to the model’s results for this sector.

Earlier studies have found that services respond strongly to rainfall. Services also make up more of richer countries’ economies, which the authors say likely helps explain their larger gains.

Farming changed little overall and lost output in richer countries during removal. Those countries cooled more sharply, which the authors suggested could bring more crop damage from frost and cold fronts.

The researchers called for removal plans to support vulnerable nations in the interests of climate justice.

They pointed to climate finance, including carbon markets and loans on easier terms, as ways to help places that would gain less.

The study followed a deliberately simple path: carbon dioxide rose and fell steadily, while everything else affecting climate stayed at 1850 levels.

Removing so much gas so quickly would create major technical and practical challenges with current technology.

The authors cautioned that their conclusions do not “represent a near-term implementation roadmap.”

They did not model any particular removal method, such as planting forests, capturing carbon dioxide directly from the air, or adding alkaline minerals to seawater.

Real projects would also need to account for their costs and energy demands.

EconClimNet assumes that past links between weather and economic output hold for nearly three centuries of simulated time.

The authors acknowledged that some apparent gains may partly reflect quirks of the model.

Its economic records cover only 77 countries, and the team left out regions without data. The model also gives limited insight into why it produces particular answers or what causes the changes it identifies.

The researchers plan to make its reasoning easier to inspect. They say further climate experiments will also help distinguish real economic gains from effects created by the model itself.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.
