#6408. Scientists just broke through a major barrier in weather forecasting

Scientists have developed an AI tool that improves weather forecasts three to four weeks ahead, offering earlier warnings of extreme weather.

Check the forecast for ten days out and you’re already taking it with a grain of salt. Past two weeks, the world’s best weather models have done worse than a simple guess that the weather will match the long-term average for that date.

A new machine-learning tool learns from past forecasting mistakes and corrects them, helping models predict broad weather patterns three to four weeks ahead more accurately than long-term averages.

The add-on doubled the skill of a leading AI weather model at those lead times.

It also improved the European model that forecasters treat as the gold standard in about nine of every ten grid squares on the map. Entered in an international competition, it beat every rival.

The team included Hannah Guan of Harvard College, Soukayna Mouatadid of the University of Toronto, Judah Cohen of MIT and Lester Mackey of Microsoft Research.

Several of the authors work at Microsoft or own its stock, and the code is free for anyone to use.

A forecast model simulates the atmosphere step by step, and small errors at each step pile up.

By the third week, accumulated errors can overwhelm the useful information in a forecast.

Forecasters call the stretch from two to six weeks out the “predictability desert.” Models there routinely score below zero on the standard skill scale, meaning a long-term average would have served you better.

Weeks three and four are also where warnings would be most useful. Three winter storms in February 2021 caused the worst energy failure in Texas history and killed at least 246 people.

Earlier warnings could have given officials more time to prepare energy systems and emergency responses.

The two-week limit goes back to MIT’s Edward Lorenz, who argued more than 50 years ago that the atmosphere is too chaotic to predict past that point. Cohen said he never fully accepted it.

The team’s tool, called probabilistic bias correction, doesn’t forecast the weather itself. It takes a model’s forecast, in the form of probabilities that a week will be unusually warm, cool, wet or dry, and adjusts those probabilities.

One half of the tool compares 20 years of the model’s past forecasts with what actually happened, spot by spot and season by season. Then it subtracts the error the model keeps making.

The other half blends the forecast with the weather observed over the past few weeks and with the long-term average. The two corrections are averaged.

The tool retrains itself every day as new forecasts and observations arrive, and it runs without a supercomputer.

“We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them,” Cohen said.

The team tested the add-on on three systems. One was the physics-based ensemble from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

The others were the center’s new AI model and a hybrid that already uses AI to clean up that ensemble.

Each system forecasts weekly temperature, rainfall and air pressure three and four weeks ahead. The scores compare those forecasts with the real weather from 2016 to 2024.

On the European ensemble, the add-on tripled the model’s small rainfall skill.

It also turned temperature and pressure forecasts that were worse than the average into ones that beat it. The center’s own daily error correction, by contrast, left rainfall skill near zero.

The add-on doubled the AI model’s average forecasting skill and improved the hybrid model’s rainfall skill by 68% to 98%, depending on the forecast period.

The biggest gains came in rainfall, which every model handles worst.

In 2025 the center opened a competition in which teams submit real-time forecasts each week.

The team entered under the name MicroDuet and finished first for every variable and both lead times in the fall season.

Behind it were the operational models of six government forecasting agencies, including NOAA in the United States, and 34 other teams.

“We consistently beat climatology averages with our models,” Cohen said. “That’s one of the more important findings, because it’s so difficult to accomplish.”

Averages matter to farmers and power companies, but the costly events are the rare ones. The team retrained the tool to flag weeks in the hottest, coldest, wettest or driest 5% for each location.

The add-on raised the European model’s skill at spotting extreme heat by 51% over the center’s standard correction. The gains were spread across most of the map rather than concentrated in a few regions.

To test performance during floods, the team examined rainfall forecasts around events recorded by an international disaster alert system over the past decade.

The add-on raised rainfall skill around those floods by 76% to 92%, while the center’s standard correction pushed it to near zero.

The 88 severe floods, those with more than 100 deaths or 80,000 people displaced, showed the biggest gains, and there the standard correction did no better than the raw model.

In November 2025, the team’s week-four forecast called for a cold outbreak across the eastern United States in mid-December. It arrived, and the European model’s corrected forecast had missed it.

“It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society,” Cohen said.

The add-on fixes the errors a model repeats. It can’t recover a signal the model never had, so the authors describe it as a post-processing step rather than a replacement for better models.

The skill scores are positive but modest: corrected forecasts performed better than long-term averages overall, but individual predictions can still be wrong.

Kenya’s meteorological office has asked about using the tool to forecast its monsoon season for farmers, Cohen said.

Evidence that a few extra weeks of warning changes what a utility or a farm actually does comes mostly from isolated case studies, the authors wrote.

The next test is whether agencies plug the code into their own models and the gains hold outside a competition.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6407. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

#6405. Planetary wreckage around a dead star may hint at Earth’s future

Mysterious rings of planetary debris around a dead star suggest that rocky worlds may survive stellar death, offering clues to Earth's distant future.

When a star like the Sun nears the end of its life, it swells dramatically, potentially swallowing the planets closest to it.

Around one dead star, though, the wreckage didn’t settle into a single ring, the way it has around every other dead star with a known gas disc. It formed two rings with a clear gap between them.

The team suspects that two rocky bodies survived the star’s transformation and that each may be supplying gas to a separate ring.

Astronomers call small rocky bodies like these planetesimals.

Nicola Gentile Fusillo, an astronomer at the University of Trieste in Italy, led the study.

“We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals,” he said.

Neither body has been seen directly. The team inferred both of them from the way the gas around the star behaves.

Near the end of its life, a star like the Sun expands and sheds its outer layers, engulfing nearby planets. Rocky bodies that survive can break apart.

Their pieces end up circling the dead star in a flat disc of dust and gas, and some of that rubble falls onto the star.

What’s left of the star itself is a white dwarf, the dense, burnt-out core. By the team’s estimates, this one holds about half the Sun’s mass in a ball roughly one and a half times as wide as Earth.

This white dwarf, called WD J1328–1450, became one somewhere around 73 million years ago.

The dusty disc around it is one of the brightest ever found around a white dwarf. Only a small share of these discs also contain gas. This one does.

The team studied the star with the X-shooter instrument on the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The instrument spreads a star’s light out by color. In a spinning disc of glowing gas, the gas moving toward Earth and the gas moving away split each bright line into two peaks.

All 21 gas discs known before this one show that pair of peaks. This star’s calcium and oxygen lines show four. The team matched them to two rings of gas, one inside the other.

The inner ring stretches from about 60,000 to 147,000 miles (97,000 to 237,000 km) from the star.

The outer ring starts about 234,000 miles (376,000 km) out, close to the Moon’s distance from Earth, and reaches roughly 835,000 miles (1.34 million km).

Together, the rings span a region nearly twice the Sun’s diameter.

The shape of the lines held steady between observations in 2021 and 2023, about two years apart.

Co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches is an astronomer at the University of Warwick in the UK and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile.

“The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap,” he said.

When gas drifts away from where it formed, it cools and turns back into solid grains. So the gas stays close to its source.

Around another white dwarf, SDSS J1228+1040, astronomers had already picked up a signal in the gas that repeats about every two hours.

Astronomers could explain it only with a dense solid body inside the disc, making gas as it interacts with the dust.

Gentile Fusillo’s team argues the same thing is happening here, twice. Gas made in two separate places would form two separate rings.

At such close distances, the white dwarf’s gravity places severe constraints on the size and strength of any surviving rocky body.

The inner body is probably the size of a typical asteroid, no more than about 107 miles (172 km) across. The outer one could be far bigger, as large as Pluto or even our Moon.

The gas contains calcium, oxygen, magnesium and iron, a mix that matches the rocky material in our own solar system. But magnesium glows only in the inner ring.

If the outer ring had the same balance of magnesium to calcium, the magnesium would have shown up clearly. It didn’t.

The missing magnesium is a clue, because different kinds of rock contain different amounts of it.

Earth’s mantle, the thick rocky layer under the crust, has about eight times as much magnesium as calcium. Earth’s crust has less than twice as much.

The chemical differences suggest the rings could contain material from two different rocky bodies.

Or they may have come from two layers of a single broken planet, with magnesium-rich mantle in one ring and magnesium-poor crust in the other.

“The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized,” Fusillo said.

In the far future, the Sun will become a white dwarf too, and that change may destroy Earth. The two rings also resemble the rings seen in discs around young stars, where planets are still forming.

“The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like,” Lagos-Vilches said.

The team can’t pin down the exact orbits of the two bodies.

Another setup could also produce four peaks. A single disc that bulges upward could shade the region where the gap appears to be, though no existing model of these discs supports that idea.

Two white dwarfs, each with its own disc, would need conditions the team calls extremely fine-tuned.

The star is also taking in rocky material more slowly than its bright disc would suggest. The team suspects the disc may be relatively young, with material falling onto the star for only 300,000 to 600,000 years.

Neither of the leading explanations for how gas forms in these discs can fully account for the mysterious gap between the rings.

For astronomers, that mystery opens a new window into what happens when planetary systems fall apart. Even after a star dies, the remains of its planets may have a complex story left to tell.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

#6403. A Startup Wants to Put 50,000 Mirrors in Space. The Goal: Make Sunlight Available at Night.

For $5,000 an hour, Reflect Orbital will bring you the power of the sun no matter what time of night it is. Astronomers are sounding the alarm.

With the launch of Sputnik in October 1957, humanity officially entered the satellite era, and in the ensuing decades, the thousands of satellites sent into space have drastically changed life on the ground. These sprawling networks of orbital spacecraft provide us with constant GPS navigation, communication, weather forecasting, and an unprecedented level of scientific surveys. But for ground-based astronomers, satellites have been a steadily growing headache.

Problems really started back in 2019 when SpaceX launched the first cadre of Starlink satellites, and almost immediately their immense number and brightness disrupted ground-based observations of space. Today, there are more than 11,000 Starlink satellites, and scientists worry about their impact on next-generation telescopes, including the new Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile.

Now astronomers may have an even bigger problem on their hands: Reflect Orbital. If you haven’t heard of this company, that’s not surprising. Unlike SpaceX, they currently don’t have any satellites in orbit at all, but what they plan to do with those satellites once they’re nestled within Earth’s orbit has astrophysicists begging for the federal government to intervene.

“This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Princeton University astrophysicist Gaspar Bakos told Sky & Telescope. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

So what exactly has astronomers like Bakos up in arms? Well, Reflect Orbital bills itself as a “sunlight-as-a-service” company whose constellation of 50,000 satellites, each armed with massive mirrors, directs sunlight toward dark areas of the planet. The company says users could conceivably call for sunlight on demand to power solar panels or aid in nighttime search-and-rescue operations. But this altruistic vision likely obscures more lucrative use-cases for the military. That seems especially likely given the going rate for sunlight: $5,000 an hour, according to Sky & Telescope. That price is well beyond the budget of most search-and-rescue groups.

Then there’s life on the ground. Plants and animals, humans included, depend on a day-night cycle that’s existed since Earth formed in the fiery cauldron of our star’s protoplanetary disk. Artificial sunlight could throw that rhythm off. Reflect Orbital CEO Ben Nowack dismissed these fears to the outlet Payload by saying that some people once feared light bulbs.

“I think a lot of people are scared of new things,” Nowack told Payload. “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and like, is this godly?…I think it’s a sign that we’re doing something that’s really new and really important.”

On October 10, Reflect Orbital conducted a test of its technology near the town of Independence, California. As previously noted, the company doesn’t have any satellites in space yet, so instead they used giant, angled flood lights to mimic what the beam would look like from space and invited search-and-rescue groups to the demonstration. For astronomers, the blinding light confirmed their worst fears. Those fears have only grown since mid-July, when the Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request to build a demonstration satellite called Earendil-1. The name continues the annoying trend of startups borrowing from The Lord of the Rings for their technologies.

“You might think a space mirror could illuminate a customer’s solar farm or a rescue site while leaving everything else untouched,” Macquarie University astrophysicist Richard de Grijs wrote for The Conversation. “That’s not quite how it works, because Earth’s atmosphere doesn’t respect sharp boundaries.”

A study in The Astrophysical Journal of Letters showed how molecules and aerosols would scatter this reflected sunlight, and another study detailed how a satellite with a 54-meter mirror (which is the operational goal) would still be brighter than our planet’s lone satellite if you were eight miles away from the beam. Within the beam, light would appear 40 times brighter than the moon, and the sky would be as luminous as after-sunset twilight. If Reflect Orbital reaches its planned 50,000-satellite constellation, the night sky would become three to four times brighter overall, according to the European Southern Observatory.

For now, the company is forging ahead with its plan to launch its first satellites with India’s Skyroot Aerospace, which will require authorization with the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre. This means the company could technically sidestep U.S. regulatory approval entirely.

“This whole question we have is: Who owns the night sky?” University of Alabama astronomer Michelle Wooten told Sky & Telescope. “I really feel that people should have a say on what their night sky looks like.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6402. Common blood pressure drug may activate the body’s calorie-burning fat

Scientists discover that losartan, a common blood pressure drug, may activate calorie-burning brown fat and offer unexpected health benefits.

Doctors prescribe losartan to lower blood pressure, but new research suggests the medication may have another unexpected benefit.

In the medical records of more than 100,000 cancer patients, people on the drug were more likely to have active brown fat, the kind that burns calories to make heat.

In mice and in lab-grown fat cells, losartan switched that fat on through a pathway separate from the one that lowers blood pressure.

That makes losartan a candidate for a job no approved drug does today, turning up brown fat in people.

Active brown fat has been linked to lower rates of diabetes and heart disease. The new study also found associations with lower rates of anxiety and depression.

Paul Cohen, who heads the Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism at Rockefeller University, led the work.

First author Nicolás Gómez-Banoy is an endocrinologist in his lab who also holds posts at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Weill Cornell Medicine.

The patient data can only show that losartan users had more brown fat, not that the drug caused it, and the direct tests were in mice and in cells.

Brown fat burns calories to make heat, so it takes up the sugar tracer used in PET scans. That makes it visible on the scans cancer patients get to track their disease.

The team pulled every such scan from Memorial Sloan Kettering between 2018 and 2024 and added them to an earlier set, for 101,243 patients in all.

Brown fat appeared on at least one scan in 8,897 of them, just under 9%. It was more common in women, in younger patients, and on colder days.

Each patient with brown fat was matched to roughly two without it, on age, sex, body mass index, and the outdoor temperature on the day of the scan.

The team then compared 511 diagnosis codes between the two groups. The cancer itself and its treatment were controlled for.

Of 98 diagnoses that differed between the groups, 92 were less common in people with brown fat.

The strongest were type 2 diabetes, at less than half the odds, and chronic ischemic heart disease, at about half.

Anxiety disorders and depression were on the list too, with odds about a fifth and a third lower.

“We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues,” Gómez-Banoy said.

The six diagnoses more common with brown fat were mostly skin conditions, and people with brown fat also had slightly lower bone density in the spine.

The team listed both as possible downsides to study.

A machine learning tool measured how much brown fat each person had and where.

Brown fat in the armpits was tied to the lowest odds of high blood pressure. It was also associated with the least fat around the organs, the belly fat that carries the most risk.

The team then checked 125 medications the patients were taking a month before their scan. Thirty-nine lined up with brown fat one way or the other.

Two kinds of drugs already known to dampen brown fat, beta blockers and the antidepressants called SSRIs, came out on the negative side.

Losartan and its cousin valsartan came out on the positive side: 2.4% of patients with brown fat were on losartan, against 1.9% of those without.

“The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive,” Cohen said. “We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.”

Losartan blocks a receptor for the hormone angiotensin, which is how it lowers blood pressure. In brown fat cells, it still worked after that receptor was knocked down, so the fat effect runs through something else.

The experiments pointed to a protein called PPAR-gamma, a master switch involved in regulating fat cells.

Losartan turned it on, and a chemical that blocks PPAR-gamma blunted losartan’s effect.

The version of losartan doing the work was a breakdown product that doesn’t touch the blood pressure receptor at all.

“The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies,” Gómez-Banoy said.

“That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.”

In mice, 10 days of losartan in the drinking water raised energy use and oxygen consumption. That held at room temperature and in the cold, without changing body weight or activity.

After two weeks on the drug, the brown fat between a mouse’s shoulders made more heat when it was stimulated.

Everyone in the study had cancer. Brown fat tracked with some cancers and some treatments, so the team controlled for both but can’t rule them out.

The scans were taken without any cold exposure, which likely undercounted brown fat.

A PET scan measures sugar uptake, not heat, and the two don’t always agree. The mouse experiments were small, with five to 10 animals per group, and the direct tests of the drug stop at mice.

“There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort,” Cohen said. “This is just a start.”

Whether losartan’s brown fat effect adds up to anything for a patient’s weight, blood sugar, or mood is the open question.

The researchers say prospective studies in people are needed to determine whether these effects translate into meaningful health benefits.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6401. NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

#6400. Something Was Hiding in This Ancient Roman Capital. It Took a Drought to Finally Reveal It.

Drones caught the ghostly outlines of a 2,000-year-old city—before returning greenery erased them again.

A heatwave wreaked havoc upon all facets of life in Europe to some degree this past summer, but it also provided archaeologists in Switzerland with an interesting opportunity: the chance to view ancient Roman history in an entirely fresh way. With vegetation stripped back and parched, a team researching Aventicum, a once-thriving Roman city, took to the air via drone for a bird’s-eye view of the entire site. From the new vantage point, they discovered things they simply hadn’t ever known existed.

The site in Switzerland’s state of Vaud, which is now known as Avenches, looked different in the unusually hot and dry months of July and August, allowing archaeologists to “observe remains usually invisible underground,” according to a statement from those working at the Aventicum archaeological site. The airborne exploration revealed previously unseen buried structures, redrawing the map of what was once the capital of Roman Helvetica.

“These are the richest discoveries made there in the last 50 years, at least over the last two generations of archaeologists,” said Jordan Anastassov, archaeologist for Vaud and the University of Geneva, according to Reuters.

The archaeologist said less vigorous plant growth occurs atop buried structures. Combine that with a drought-stricken region and wilting vegetation this past summer, and the archaeologists were able to make a number of “observations that complement the data from the excavations in an exceptional way and show the full potential of surface prospecting methods.”

Aerial images not only showed the locations of houses (making up a full neighborhood), expansive villas, and roads, but also highlighted thermal baths and a potential rectangular temple site running nearly 100 feet in length that was lost to history. Some of the buildings appear in sections of the historic city that haven’t been excavated, and the large building sits on what was once thought to be the town’s outskirts.

Founded originally after Julius Caesar conquered local tribes 2,000 years ago, Aventicum had a successful run under Roman rule, eventually succumbing to Germanic invasions, starting in the third century. “We are now asking really interesting questions we wouldn’t otherwise be asking,” said Hugo Amoroso, an archaeologist on the project.

The team hopes on-the-ground exploration of the newly discovered areas will provide fuller detail and a richer history.

The summer heat proved critical in exposing the areas. By September, as temperatures returned to normal and vegetation started to flourish again, many of the newly seen sites slipped from view, although the pools discovered at the bath location were still visible in a struggling alfalfa field. “We aren’t going to wish for droughts,” said Pierre Blanc, director of the site’s excavations, “but we’re going to make the most of this and keep looking.”

The use of droughts to reveal lost sites isn’t a new concept. Going aerial simply helps cover more ground quickly. A post from the tourism website About Switzerland that Anastassov shared on his LinkedIn page noted that a 1976 drought played a role in the discovery of a Roman villa in the nearby municipality of Orbe.

With droughts increasing throughout the world, archaeologists are turning to aerial monitoring as a planned tactic, scheduling surveys systematically to better understand potential excavation sites and more accurately redraw ancient maps, just like at Aventicum.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6399. Scientists uncover a troubling pattern beneath Earth’s frozen ground

A global study of 156 monitoring sites reveals widespread permafrost thaw, raising concerns about infrastructure, carbon emissions, and climate change.

Every summer for the past three decades, Anna Klene has driven north across Alaska’s Brooks Range, and pushed a metal rod into the ground.

She records the depth at which it hits frozen earth. Then she moves on to the next site, and the next. It’s not glamorous science.

“It’s not super sophisticated,” she said. “You push down on the probe, put your finger on the rod and you can measure how many centimeters into the ground it went.”

These simple, long-term measurements have now produced something significant: the first global assessment of long-term permafrost monitoring data.

The findings confirm what climate scientists have feared. Permafrost is thawing broadly, persistently, and in ways that matter far beyond the frozen ground itself.

The measurement Klene takes is called active layer thickness. It refers to the depth of the ground above permafrost that freezes and thaws each year.

In a stable system, that layer stays roughly constant from one decade to the next.

When it deepens over time, it can signal that the underlying permafrost is warming and becoming less stable.

Permafrost is not simply frozen dirt. It’s soil, rock, and sediment bound together by ice that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years. In many places, that happened for thousands of years.

Permafrost underlies 15 percent of exposed land surface in the Northern Hemisphere and almost all of Antarctica’s ice-free areas.

And it holds something that makes its stability a matter of global consequence. Roughly 70 percent of the organic carbon stored in permafrost soils sits in just the top three meters.

As the ground thaws, microbes can break down previously frozen organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere.

The study draws on data from 156 monitoring sites gathered between 2000 and 2024. The average record length per site is 20 years.

The pattern is consistent and troubling. Active layer thickness increased significantly at 55 percent of Arctic sites and 38 percent of Antarctic sites.

In mountain permafrost regions over 90 percent of sites showed significant increases. Several sites saw the active layer double in thickness over the study period.

At two Norwegian mountain sites, Juvvasshøe and Snøheim, the active layer increased by 8.45 centimeters per year. At Swiss Alpine sites, increases of 9 to 36 centimeters per year were recorded.

In the Arctic lowlands, sites with thick organic layers, including peatlands and densely vegetated areas, showed smaller increases.

That happens because the insulating properties of organic matter buffer the soil against air temperature swings.

It is the bare, sandy, and bedrock sites that are changing fastest. Alaska’s North Slope recorded active layer increases at most sites between 0.3 and 0.6 centimeters per year.

Sites previously impacted by wildfires showed larger increases, because fire removes the insulating vegetation layer, exposing frozen ground directly to summer warmth.

“One of Earth’s most important indicators of climate change is permafrost as it directly reacts to rising temperatures,” said lead author Dmitry Streletskiy, a geography professor at George Washington University.

“The significance of this study lies in the fact that we’re not just looking at isolated hotspots anymore.”

The regression analysis behind the study found that summer warmth is the dominant driver of active layer change in Arctic lowland permafrost.

Total liquid precipitation has a smaller but significant additional effect: wet summers deepen the thaw more than dry ones. Cold seasons, by contrast, have minimal influence once site-specific characteristics are controlled for.

Mountain permafrost behaves differently and is harder to model. The sites are highly heterogeneous and the available climate data at high elevations isn’t fine-grained enough to fully explain everything.

Some mountain sites, particularly in the Swiss Alps, are changing at rates that dwarf anything seen in the Arctic lowlands.

The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in China deserves particular attention.

Active layer changes on the Third Pole – so called because it holds more ice than anywhere on Earth outside the polar regions – averaged 3.2 centimeters per year from 2000 to 2024.

That’s roughly four times the Arctic average for continuous permafrost.

The plateau is warming faster than almost anywhere else on the planet, and it sits beneath infrastructure that crosses some of the most challenging terrain in the world.

Permafrost degradation is not an abstract threat.

Roads, railways, airports, pipelines, and buildings across northern Alaska, Canada, Siberia, and the Tibetan Plateau are built on the assumption that the ground beneath them stays frozen.

When it doesn’t, foundations shift, roads buckle, and infrastructure built over decades requires expensive repair or abandonment.

Communities in northern Alaska have already been forced to consider relocation as coastlines destabilize and the ground under their homes subsides.

“It’s hard to see that the first frost and the first snow are shifting by a day or two a decade,” Klene said.

“It’s hard to see that kind of change and really appreciate that it will have a big impact over time. But with these long-term monitoring sites, we can see that this gradual change is happening, and it’s going to affect the whole system.”

That system includes the carbon cycle. Continued warming threatens to shrink the extent of permafrost worldwide, with consequences that could unfold for generations.

What that means in terms of carbon release remains one of the largest uncertainties in climate science.

The study is published in the journal Communications: Earth and Environment.

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

#6397. Astronomers found the first star that would look green to the human eye

Astronomers have identified the first known green star, a white dwarf tinted by sodium from planetary debris, alongside unusually colored stars.

A dead star called WD J1330+6435 is the first known star that would appear green to human eyes. Astronomers at the University of Warwick identified it while working out the true colors of nearby white dwarfs.

The star’s green tint comes from sodium in rocky material it has pulled in from its own planetary system. That sodium absorbs the orange part of the star’s light.

The same work flagged WD J1011+2845, just 48 light-years from Earth, as what may be the reddest star ever recorded.

White dwarfs are the dense remnants left behind when Sun-like stars reach the end of their lives. None is close enough for its color to be seen directly.

The researchers worked from each star’s spectrum, the pattern produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, and ran those spectra through a model of human color vision.

The sample covered the 151 white dwarfs within 20 parsecs, or about 65 light-years, of Earth.

The results correct a common misconception in astronomy that white dwarfs are typically blue. Hotter, bluer white dwarfs are brighter, so surveys based on brightness alone over-represent them.

Dr. Mark Hollands, a Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group at the university, led the work.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their colour is set almost entirely by temperature,” Hollands said.

“It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colours nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me,” he added.

WD J1330+6435 has a temperature of roughly 7,200°F (4,000°C). It has accreted rocky material from its planetary system, enriching its atmosphere with calcium, lithium and sodium.

The atmospheres of these stars can reach roughly the density of water, millions of times denser than the Sun’s visible surface, the university explained.

Because this star’s atmosphere is so dense, the sodium absorbs light across a broad range of yellow, orange and red wavelengths. What remains gives the star a chartreuse green appearance in the team’s models.

As far as the researchers are aware, no other star, living or dead, has ever been credibly reported as green. That makes WD J1330+6435 the first known genuinely green star in the Galaxy.

“Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star,” Hollands noted. “It feels like something out of science fiction.”

White dwarfs that pull in the remains of planets carry elements such as lithium, sodium and calcium in their atmospheres, where astronomers can read them in starlight.

In 2021, Hollands and his colleagues reported lithium in four cool, old white dwarfs with cooling ages of five to ten billion years. WD J1330+6435, catalogued then as SDSS J1330+6435, was one of the four.

That work placed the star about 87 parsecs, or roughly 280 light-years, from Earth.

The amounts of lithium and potassium compared with sodium and calcium “strongly suggest that all four white dwarfs have accreted fragments of planetary crusts,” the authors wrote in Nature Astronomy.

Another star in that set, WD J2317+1830, also showed extra infrared light, a sign that it was still drawing material from a surrounding disk of dust and rock.

In the new color study, white dwarfs enriched with fragments of shattered asteroids and comets tend toward yellow. Carbon-rich white dwarfs are typically pink or purple.

In WD J0902+2010, the convection zone has reached the core and lifted interior carbon to the surface. There, carbon forms C2 molecules that absorb blue, green and yellow light, so the star would look pink to the human eye.

WD J1011+2845 goes further. Carbon molecules distort its light so heavily that almost all of it is squeezed into wavelengths beyond 600 nanometers, producing a deep salmon-pink glow.

Cooler white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres often take on a cyan or pale blue tinge. That color comes from hydrogen molecules colliding with helium atoms in their ultra-dense atmospheres.

Sirius B, the nearest white dwarf to the Solar System, has a hot hydrogen atmosphere that gives it a bluish color in the models.

Of the 151 nearby white dwarfs, five showed unusual coloring: two yellow and three pink. That suggests roughly one in 30 white dwarfs in the Universe shines with an unusually colored light.

For the remaining 146 stars, the median color temperature was about 6,800 kelvin, roughly 11,800°F (6,530°C), which people perceive as white.

Professor Boris Gänsicke of the Department of Physics at Warwick co-authored the study.

“One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly coloured stars out there,” Gänsicke said.

“Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white,” he explained.

The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

#6396. Researchers found a crushed Celtic helmet in Poland that proves wealthy southerners traveled along the Amber Route

A crushed Celtic helmet lay in a charred pit at Łysa Góra, Poland, with four iron adzes, a scythe and nearly 350 metal finds from the site.

Łysa Góra is a glacial sand dune between the Orzyc River and one of its oxbow lakes, near the village of Bagienice in northern Mazovia, Poland.

Inside its fortifications, archaeologists found a pit filled with charred remains that held a crushed bronze helmet, four iron adzes and an iron scythe.

The helmet is a Berru-type helmet of La Tène (Celtic) origin. Five authors, Kaczyński, Maciałowicz, Borkowski, Sobczak and Aniszewski, described the find in Antiquity on October 14, 2026.

They propose that people from the Celtic south may have been on the dune themselves. The idea has not been tested yet.

The name means Bald Hill. From the sixth to the fourth century BC, members of the West Balt Barrow Culture lived on the dune.

According to the paper, these communities built fortified sites, lived off rivers and lakes, and buried their dead together in urns.

Archaeologists logged the site in 1957 and dug it in short bursts between 1971 and 1992. Those digs recovered several La Tène imports. No full analysis was ever published, so the paper says the site’s importance went unnoticed.

In 2024 the State Archaeological Museum in Warsaw and the Faculty of Archaeology at the University of Warsaw resumed the work. Kaczyński, Borkowski, Sobczak and Aniszewski work at the museum. Maciałowicz is at the university.

The pit lay within the fortifications. The authors found the helmet crushed and fragmented, lying alongside several iron tools, including adzes and a scythe. They read the pit as one of the traces of ritual activity at the site.

The paper’s plan view of the pit, based on a photograph by Kaczyński, numbers the helmet, the scythe and four adzes marked 3a to 3d. The helmet closely parallels finds from Dürrnberg in Austria.

Two kinds of timber-and-earth defenses guarded the dune around the middle of the first millennium BC. In the south, a rampart with a palisade and an outer ditch was cut partly into the natural sediment. In the north, the team found a fortification built entirely of timber.

A second ritual zone lay in the marsh at the foot of the dune’s southwestern slope. Two deposits there held bronze ring ornaments and earrings with glass beads.

One deposit included a spiral armlet made of bronze ribbon and decorated with incised lines. The team found traces of repair on one end, where two rivets once sat and left circular holes. B. Karch drew a reconstruction of the armlet.

Nearly 350 metal objects have come out of the ground so far, among them ornaments, weapons and evidence of bronze working. Pottery, animal bones, cereal grains, seeds of cultivated plants and charred wood turned up as well.

Many of the bronze ornaments were broken into pieces and packed into tight bundles. The authors think they were prepared for remelting, and excavators had already recorded ceramic casting crucibles in the 1970s.

The site also yielded amber beads and an amber ring that was never finished. The authors say these finds suggest the people on the dune took part in long-distance amber exchange with regions south of the Carpathian Mountains.

Amber was prized in northern Europe long before: in Karelia, a 5,400-year-old grave held 140 amber ornaments.

The team also looked at the carbonized wood left in the socket of one iron adze. Under the microscope, a cross-section showed pores arranged in rings and both very wide and narrow wood rays, which are features of oak.

The dune has also given up 31 mostly broken Early La Tène brooches and ring ornaments, dated to around the middle of the fourth century BC.

According to the paper, helmets in the Early La Tène world symbolised “high social status and affiliation with the warrior elite.”

The authors consider that concept likely alien to the local societies, which were presumably without centralized leaders.

For that reason they argue the helmet may reflect “the physical presence of southern groups, including members of their elite.”

Trade from hand to hand is the alternative, since smaller La Tène ornaments did reach distant parts of Central and Eastern Europe.

The authors find that explanation less convincing, because the helmet was a prestige object and no comparable helmets are known outside the La Tène zone in the fourth century BC.

The dune lies close to the amber-rich Kurpie region, and the paper ties it to routes that led to the Sambian Peninsula on the Baltic coast.

Most Celtic sites of that age lie well to the south and west. Road surveyors in the Czech Republic found a lost Celtic town full of gold, silver and amber, and in central France, archaeologists dug up 2,300-year-old Celtic swords adorned with gems and symbols.

The authors say their hypothesis “will require verification through further research.” The ore source of the helmet’s metal is not yet known.

Lead isotope analyses are planned, and the results will be compared with similar objects from Bohemia, where a 2021 study of the Duchcov hoard examined Celtic movements in the fourth century BC.

The northern and southern defensive lines may or may not have stood at the same time. The team plans electrical resistivity tomography and magnetic surveys to check.

Money for the project came from the museum, the Chorzele commune authorities and the Faculty of Archaeology. The lead isotope results are still to come. Until then the helmet only points south, and nobody can say who put it in the pit.

The full study was published in the journal Antiquity.

#6395. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

#6394. Divers Spent 7 Years Hunting a Ghost Ship Linked to a Nazi Spy Plot. They Just Found It.

A citizen-led search found the SS Cornwallis—and revived a forgotten Nazi spy story in Maine.

For seven years, a group of volunteer divers scoured historical records and the coast of Maine in search of one of New England’s largest undiscovered World War II shipwrecks. Now the SS Cornwallis has been found. The Nomad Exploration Team located the Canadian merchant vessel, which a German U-boat sank off Mount Desert Rock in 1944. The discovery also helps tell the story of the 43 people aboard the boat who lost their lives in the attack and revives interest in the German spies linked to the sinking.

The team used side-scan sonar to map the ocean floor where they believed the Cornwallis might rest, and they nearly overlooked the 400-foot, 5,458-ton vessel. Some of the group’s most harrowing dives later confirmed that the sonar anomaly really was the lost ship. “It was exhilaration,” said Danny Allan, a founding team member, according to Seacoastonline.

The nine-member, New Hampshire-based team began the search in 2019 with a rough location about 10 miles southwest of Mount Desert Rock. By drawing on historical records, the ship’s blueprints, and local fishermen’s observations, they narrowed the search to three likely sites. Even so, the work wasn’t going to be easy.

“There are big tides up off the Mount Desert area,” team member Jeff Goodreau told the Portland Press Herald. “A lot of weather, a lot of fog … Any way you look at it, the challenge is just getting there, whether it’s a five-hour run from Portsmouth or trailering a boat up there.”

In fact, the team nearly missed the wreck twice. On a first pass within 300 feet of it, they didn’t recognize the sonar image. Later, while they were reprogramming the GPS, they almost skipped past it again when it showed up just 100 feet away. “We would’ve written off that whole section as ‘we already looked there’ and wouldn’t have found it,” Allan said.

Reaching the wreck, nearly 400 feet down, was just as tricky. Team member Don Ferrara called it the scariest dive he’d ever done, and Goodreau described the site as deep, cold, and full of current. Still, “We were over the moon,” Ferrara said of the find.

“You’re the first person to see and touch this wreck literally in 80 years, so you’re ecstatic,” Allan said. “But it’s also extremely sobering because this is a grave. 43 souls lost their lives on this wreck.”

The tragedy happened in the Gulf of Maine as the Canadian ship was heading home to Saint John, New Brunswick, after loading sugar and molasses in Barbados. At 6 a.m. on December 3, 1944, the German submarine U-1230 fired a single torpedo that struck the forward cargo hold, and the Cornwallis sank in less than 10 minutes, according to the team. Only five of the 48 people aboard, most of them Canadian, survived. Fishing boats picked up the survivors, and a U.S. Navy vessel then carried them to Rockland, Maine.

The Cornwallis wasn’t a target the U-boat had been hunting. “The U-boat wasn’t looking for them,” Ferrara said. “They were just there.”

The sinking alerted the U.S. to the U-boat’s presence and prompted an investigation into its mission. By interviewing witnesses in Hancock, the FBI learned about Germany’s Operation Elster (Operation Magpie in English). Just days before the attack, the same submarine had landed two German spies, Erich Gimpel and William Colepaugh, near Hancock Point. Their mission was to gather intelligence in the United States. The pair took a taxi to Bangor, a train to Portland, and then made their way to New York City. In the end, the plot fell apart from within: Colepaugh lost his nerve, confided in a friend, and turned himself in, which led to both men’s capture.

This wasn’t the first time the Cornwallis had been torpedoed. The ship was built in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1921. In 1942, a torpedo struck it while it was anchored at Barbados, and it partially sank in shallow water. After repairs, it returned to service.

“For the team, finding the wreck was the culmination of years of persistence,” Allan said in a statement, according to MassLive. “For the families and communities connected to the ship, it brings renewed attention to a largely forgotten tragedy.”

The Cornwallis is the latest find for the team, which had already located the USS Eagle 56 and the SS William H. Machen. “I love history,” Allan said. “My father was a history teacher. Other people like to see pretty fish and reefs. For me, I love to go see wrecks.”
