#6393. A ranching couple took photos of rock spires carved from ancient ash and helped create Chiricahua National Park

A 27-million-year-old eruption left a caldera 12 miles wide in Arizona. Its rock spires, protected since 1924, are now Chiricahua National Park.

Around 1900, a teenager named Ed Riggs climbed Sugarloaf Mountain, in what is now Chiricahua National Park in southeastern Arizona. He was hiking with Ben Erickson, aged nine, the brother of the woman he would later marry. From the top they looked down on a canyon full of rock pinnacles.

Ed only got to explore it after World War I, when he came home from the Army. The pinnacles are what is left of ash from a volcano that erupted about 27 million years ago.

On October 20, 2026, President Donald J. Trump signed the Chiricahua National Park Act. It turned the monument that Ed and his wife Lillian pushed for into a national park.

NASA published a Landsat 9 image of it on October 28, but the change is to the name and status, not to the trails or the scenic drive.

Ed came from a ranching family in the Sulphur Springs Valley. He served in the war as an aerial photographer. The National Park Service page on Ed Riggs quotes him calling the canyon “some of the most wonderful country.”

Lillian was the daughter of Swedish homesteaders Neil and Emma Erickson. She taught school until about 1918. That year she and her sister Hildegard named the family place Faraway Ranch, the NPS profile of Lillian Erickson Riggs says.

In the summer of 1921 Lillian was in Los Angeles, trying to start a writing career. Ed helped out at the ranch and wrote to her about a big house in the upper garden “to take care of the tourist trade.” They married on February 26, 1923.

The couple cut trails into the rocks and took photographs. Some of the pictures went to the county fair in Douglas, where a Dr. J.J.P. Armstrong saw them and came out to look for himself.

He and Ed explored the side canyons together. The park service says they were probably among the first non-Indigenous people to see Natural Bridge and Echo Canyon.

In August 1923, Arizona Governor George W.P. Hunt rode out on horseback in pouring rain from Faraway Ranch into the Chiricahua National Forest. Ed wrote afterward that the party came back “a wet bunch I can tell you but well pleased with what they had seen.”

Hunt backed a monument on the Forest Service land. President Calvin Coolidge established Chiricahua National Monument on April 18, 1924. Ed and Lillian then advertised Faraway Ranch as the closest place to stay.

In the Depression, Ed took a job with the Civilian Conservation Corps as a local trail foreman, at $1,800 a year. Lillian kept running the cattle and the guests.

Ed built the Sugarloaf Trail, with a tunnel blasted through rock. Then he asked Frank Pinkley, superintendent of Southwestern National Monuments, to let him route a trail down to Echo Park.

Pinkley agreed, but told him that if he failed he should “just hand in your resignation.” The Echo Canyon Trail needed eleven switchbacks in one quarter-mile.

In 1934 the monument passed to the National Park Service. More than 6,000 people in about 1,000 cars came to the dedication at Massai Point, according to the NPS history of Massai Point.

A 1997 U.S. Geological Survey guide dates the eruption to 26.9 million years ago. Its authors were John S. Pallister and Edward A. du Bray of the USGS and Douglas B. Hall of the University of Arizona.

According to the guide, magma pooled a few miles down, just south of today’s park. The rock on top broke and gas escaped. The foaming magma swelled up to 50 times its volume in a series of explosions.

More than 100 cubic miles (over 400 cubic kilometers) of magma came out. Hot ash and pumice covered at least 1,200 square miles (3,100 square kilometers).

Mount St. Helens put out about a tenth of a cubic mile in 1980. The empty chamber’s roof caved in and left the Turkey Creek caldera, 12 miles (19 kilometers) wide and at least 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) deep.

Ash of a similar age elsewhere in the West kept other records. At John Day Fossil Beds in Oregon, 29-million-year-old ash holds paw tracks left by a cat with retractable claws.

Calderas can matter for other reasons too, and the McDermitt caldera on the Nevada-Oregon border may hold a large lithium deposit.

In the park area the ash filled an old valley at least 1,600 feet (490 meters) deep. It was hot enough to weld into solid rock. The layer is known as the Rhyolite Canyon Tuff, named for the canyon where it is best exposed.

The tuff cracked along vertical joints as it cooled. Water got in, froze and thawed, and pried the blocks apart, the NPS Geodiversity Atlas says.

What stayed standing became pinnacles, columns and balanced rocks. Mind you, the USGS guide thinks the columns we see today are less than three million years old, a fraction of the tuff’s age.

NASA’s satellite singles out Big Balanced Rock, where a large boulder sits perched on top. Civilian Conservation Corps crews named many of the formations in the 1930s, the park service says. The Chiricahua Apache, whose homeland this is, already called the area the Land of the Standing-Up Rocks.

The Operational Land Imager on Landsat 9 took the NASA picture on July 2, 2026. Lauren Dauphin of the NASA Earth Observatory processed it. The worn tuff looks gray, and Rhyolite Canyon and Bonita Canyon show up as green lines of trees.

The Chiricahua Mountains are one of the sky islands of southern Arizona, ranges that stand alone above the desert. Sky islands in other places have their own residents, like the four new chameleons described from Mozambique’s sky islands.

NASA’s write-up, by Adam Voiland, says four regions meet in the park, from the Sonoran Desert to the Sierra Madre. About 1,000 plant species grow there, from agaves and prickly pear to pine, fir and oak.

The Interior Department release describes a park of about 12,000 acres. Nowhere does it give figures for staff, money or expected visitors.

Jessica Bowron, who is exercising the authority of the National Park Service director, said that while the name is changing, the agency’s commitment stays the same.

From orbit, single spires are too small to pick out, NASA notes, so the gray patch in the image is the tuff as a whole.

Lillian Riggs went blind in 1942 and closed the guest ranch in 1970. She sold most of the Stafford land and cabin to the park service in 1968 and the rest of the homestead in 1974. She died in 1977, after moving to a nursing home in Willcox.

Ed died in 1950. His gravestone says he engineered the Echo Trail, and it adds, “He wished this to be his monument.” The trail still winds through the spires he first saw from Sugarloaf as a boy.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

#6391. November 2026: What’s in the sky this month?

Saturn is already visible as darkness falls; some challenging transits of its moons occur this month. Neptune is a binocular object close to Saturn, while Uranus is an easy target in Taurus. A Full Moon courses in front of the Pleiades in late November. Mars and Jupiter dominate the early-morning sky, and in the hour before dawn, look also for Venus and Mercury.

Neptune and Saturn are well placed for observation after sunset. They’re about 7° apart all month, with Neptune in southern Pisces and Saturn just across the border in Cetus. Only Saturn is visible to the naked eye, shining at magnitude 0.5. Neptune, at magnitude 7.7, requires binoculars to spot.

Swing 7×50 binoculars one field of view west of Saturn and look for a parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars: 27, 29, 30, and 33 Piscium. Neptune is within 3° northeast of 29 Psc all month. A waning gibbous Moon hangs 5° northwest of Neptune’s location on the 19th. The following night, Saturn is 6° south of the Moon.

As the month opens, Saturn is 24° high in the east an hour after sunset, reaching 50° by 9 p.m. local time following its opposition last month. It’s observable overnight and by the end of November sets by 2 a.m. local time. The rings are angled 6° to our line of sight and reveal their southern side. The planet spans 19″ through a telescope and the disk exhibits a pale yellowish hue. Atmospheric details are tricky to spot unless you have very good conditions.

Titan, Saturn’s brightest moon (magnitude 8.3), sits closest to the planet Nov. 8 and 24 (north), and Nov. 16 (south). Tenth-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea orbit closer in. Dione and Tethys transit Saturn’s disk this month. These transits and shadow transits are extremely challenging. They’re good targets for advanced observers with video imaging experience. Visit Astronomy.com for more details on the timing of their transits if you’d like to try for them.

Iapetus reaches greatest eastern elongation Nov. 10, when it stands 9.4′ east of Saturn. The moon’s darker face is turned earthward, dimming it to magnitude 11.9. It’s hard to find but as the month progresses, Iapetus brightens nearly a magnitude by the time it reaches inferior conjunction early on the 30th, 1.7′ due north of Saturn.

Uranus remains midway between Aldebaran and the Pleiades (M45). This position makes the planet easier to find than in previous years. It reaches opposition Nov. 25, visible from dusk to dawn. From 1.71 billion miles away, its disk spans 4″. Uranus shines at magnitude 5.6, within easy range of binoculars and potentially visible to the unaided eye from the darkest skies.

To find Uranus, look between Aldebaran and M45 for two stars: 37 and 39 Tauri (4.5° southeast of M45). Brighter 37 Tau glows at magnitude 4.4. On Nov. 1, Uranus is 1.6° southeast of 37 Tau, and by the end of November stands 1.5° due south of this star. Another star, some 2.7° southeast of 37 Tau, shines at magnitude 5.5. This is 43 Tau; in mid-November, Uranus is halfway between the two stars.

The Full Moon crosses the Pleiades early on Nov. 24, setting up a series of occultations of the northern part of the cluster just before dawn across the western half of the U.S. You’ll need a telescope — plan for higher magnification so you can place the brilliant Moon largely out of your field of view. Fifth-magnitude Celaeno is the first of the cluster’s brighter stars to be occulted, around 6 a.m. CST. Both visibility and timing heavily depend on your location, so set up at least 30 minutes before the event starts. You can download timings for the brightest occultations from 40 major North American cities from the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Mars and Jupiter rise close together in Leo. They meet in a conjunction midmonth not far from Leo’s brightest star, Regulus. Mars rises first, soon after midnight on the 1st, followed by Jupiter about 30 minutes later. Jupiter shines at magnitude –2.0 and Mars at 0.8. They’re hard to miss.

On Nov. 1, Jupiter stands midway between Mars and Regulus, each just over 5° from its neighbor. A waning gibbous Moon sits in Cancer only a few degrees west of M44, the Beehive star cluster. On the 2nd, Mars and the Moon are 1.5° apart, and by the 3rd the Moon lies less than 2° from Regulus as they rise in the Midwest. Mars and Jupiter close in on each other, and by the 15th Mars is 1.2° due north of Jupiter.

Mars continues eastward, reaching a point 1.7° due north of Regulus on the 25th. By the 30th, Mars is just over 2° northeast of Regulus and is rejoined by the waning gibbous Moon, just southwest of Regulus. Through a telescope at the end of November, Mars has reached 8″ in diameter and its magnitude has increased to 0.4.

Home to the most visibly dynamic atmosphere in the solar system, Jupiter has a lot to offer through a telescope. The planet shows off a 36″-wide disk on the 1st, which grows to 39″ by the 30th. The hour before dawn can hold remarkable views if there is steady seeing. Look for the occasional appearance of the Great Red Spot.

Jupiter’s moons and their shadows often transit the planet or are eclipsed by it. Nov. 8 finds Io and Callisto transiting Jupiter’s disk along with Io’s shadow. Soon after, Europa exits from an occultation. East Coast observers will see the whole event; the Pacific Coast, only the latter half. It begins as Io’s shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb at 1:29 a.m. EST, followed 24 minutes later by the reappearance of Europa from behind Jupiter. Callisto’s transit begins at 2:07 a.m. EST. Io approaches the eastern limb, passing due north of Europa at 2:23 a.m. EST and beginning its transit 19 minutes later. Because of Io’s faster orbital speed compared with Callisto, it overtakes the larger moon within half an hour. Io’s shadow exits the disk at 3:45 a.m. EST, and Io itself ends its transit 74 minutes later. Callisto’s transit ends at 5:51 a.m. CST, as the sky is growing light in the Midwest.

Ganymede’s huge shadow crosses Jupiter’s face Nov. 11. The start of the transit at 12:27 a.m. EST is visible from the Eastern time zone; it ends at 4:03 a.m. EST, visible across the U.S. Ganymede begins to transit at 5:29 a.m. EST.

Ganymede, Europa, and Io orbit in resonance, so similar events recur, although they are not always observable. On Nov. 15, Io’s shadow begins a transit at 3:22 a.m. EST. Europa reappears at 4:27 a.m. EST, with Io close to the limb. They pass north-south just seven minutes later. Io’s transit begins at 4:36 a.m. EST. Its shadow leaves at 5:38 a.m. EST, and Io departs at 5:52 a.m. CST (in daylight for EST). Ganymede’s shadow transits again three days later, Nov. 18, from 4:25 a.m. EST to 6:01 a.m. MST (note the time zone change).

On Nov. 22, Io and its shadow are already transiting by the time Europa reappears. Io’s shadow transit starts at 5:15 a.m. EST; Io follows at 5:29 a.m. CST, with the sky very bright along the East Coast. Europa reappears at Jupiter’s eastern limb at 6:00 a.m. CST, as twilight begins in the Midwest and visible in darkness farther west.

To cap off the month, watch Ganymede reappear from behind Jupiter Nov. 29 at 5:53 a.m. CST (minutes before sunrise in EST), followed by Io’s shadow transit starting a few minutes later, at 6:08 a.m. CST. Io is due north of Ganymede at 6:49 a.m. CST, seen in twilight in the Midwest.

Mercury is at inferior conjunction Nov. 4, then moves into the morning sky. Northern Hemisphere observers gain good views in the second half of the month. Look for it Nov. 13, when it’s magnitude 0.5. An hour before sunrise, it is 4° high in the eastern sky, nearly 13° to the lower left of Venus. Swing binoculars toward Mercury to spot 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis 0.9° north of the planet.

Mercury reaches its greatest western elongation 20° from the Sun late on Nov. 20. The next morning, it shines at magnitude –0.5 and stands 7° high an hour before sunrise, easy to spot with a clear eastern horizon. Mercury displays a 62%-lit globe when viewed with a telescope, though it spans only 7″, so you’ll need steady air to see the phase. That phase grows to 84% by Nov. 30.

On Nov. 4, look for Venus 2° south of 1st-magnitude Spica, Virgo’s brightest star. A 25-day-old crescent Moon stands high above the pair. Three days later, on Nov. 7, Venus, Spica, and the Moon lie close together in the morning sky. Venus is 1.3° from Spica, with the waning crescent Moon about 2° below Venus, a stunning view in the brightening twilight. Venus rises about 100 minutes before the Sun and the trio is 11° high at 6 a.m. local time.

Venus reaches a stationary point Nov. 11. From the 10th to the 12th, Venus appears not to move in right ascension relative to Spica, as the planet slides due north to stand 1.2° due west of Spica on the 10th.

Check out Venus with a telescope. The bright planet becomes easier on the eyes as twilight grows, reducing the contrast. It’s already dazzling at magnitude –4.2 on the 1st, when its disk is 3% lit. By Nov. 15 it is 14% lit and magnitude –4.8, and reaches its greatest illuminated extent Nov. 29 at magnitude –4.9 and 27% lit. If you’re under Bortle 1 or 2 skies, can you see your shadow? Venus rises more than three hours before the Sun, so you’ll have a dark sky for an hour or so to check.

Much of the Moon’s history is encapsulated in one feature: the crater Schickard, way down in the lunar southwest. Protective measures are necessary to comfortably carry out this observation. Screw in a dark filter, mask off part of your scope’s aperture, or pump up the magnification to reduce the glare of an almost full lunar disk.

Start on the evening of the 21st, when the rays of sunlight strike the flooded crater at a glancing angle, highlighting the differences in height of the smaller features. This is an old crater, its rounded rim pounded down across the ages. The splatter of smaller craters across the smooth floor sport the classic sharp edges of relative youth. The western wall, steep at the instant of formation, slumped abruptly down into terraces that remain visible to this day. Shadows disappear over the next two evenings as the climbing Sun almost erases these features.

During the following nights, Schickard transforms into a two-faced striped crater, an unusual swath of lighter gray painted across the middle of this time-worn feature. The 130-mile-wide depression was carved out some 4 billion years ago as bombardment was ending. Lava soon welled up and covered its central peaks. Then the giant Orientale impact event to the west sprayed the whole region with lighter-hued material. A final surge of lava managed to cover the northern and southern portions, but did not rise enough to erase the lighter stripe.

This year’s annual Leonid meteor shower is active from Nov. 6 to 30 and peaks Nov. 17/18. A nine-day-old gibbous Moon sets right around midnight on this night, favoring the best time for meteor observing, which is after midnight. That’s when we’re on the leading hemisphere as Earth plows into the meteoroid stream.

Leo is also rising around local midnight and the radiant, located in the Sickle asterism, climbs to more than 60° in altitude by dawn. But don’t look at the radiant — meteors come head-on from that direction. Longer trails occur 40° to 60° away from Leo.

Rates are predicted to be 15 meteors per hour if the radiant were overhead. If you get more than a half-dozen per hour, you’re doing well. If you want a change, spend some time with Jupiter (also in Leo) through a telescope — Ganymede’s shadow is transiting the morning of the 18th.

The Leonids are known to be swift and some leave glowing, persistent trains, which are fascinating to experience. The shower is associated with Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which last reached perihelion in 1998.

Comet 10P/Tempel is floating halfway between Fomalhaut and Beta (β) Ceti. It’s about 10th magnitude, but historically has had post-perihelion outbursts, which could help it shine through the thicker air near the ground.

Meanwhile, Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS is higher and in a more interesting sky as darkness settles.

The Moon-free window closes after the 14th but reopens on the 27th. To see this 10th-magnitude fuzzy, a site well away from city lights is needed. Despite Earth’s increasing distance, the comet is sunward bound for perihelion Nov. 27, so its magnitude is fairly constant.

The short, broad fan should sport a circular green coma that looks great on images as it floats across the rich Milky Way north of Altair. At month’s end, Hartley-IRAS lies within 3° of the Coathanger asterism. Visually, a 4-inch scope can pull it in, but a larger one will show more detail, especially the sharp south flank where the solar wind pushes away the expelled dust in a bow shock.

Discovered in 1983, the comet returns every 21.5 years. Next month will be our last chance for a good look until two revolutions down the road, in 2069.

With five minutes of dark adapting, it’s easy to follow a main-belt asteroid along a retrograde curve. Saturn leads the way to 4 Vesta in the midevening sky — just drop down 9°, two binocular fields, to 25 Ceti, a magnitude 5.4 candle compared to the other nearby 8th- to 9th-magnitude stellar points. None of those will get confused with the brighter asteroid.

Use 25 Ceti and the more northerly 20 Ceti (closer to Saturn) to anchor a sketch or your memory. Watch a simple hockey stick pattern morph every three nights or so into a golf club, and then become a vertical line.

Spanning about 320 miles, Vesta is the second-largest body in the main belt. It was initially thought to be a chunk of the “missing” world astronomers expected between Mars and Jupiter. We now know it is an unfinished building block left over from the formation of the solar system, a rocky mantle surrounding an iron core.

The map below portrays the sky as seen near 35° north latitude. Located inside the border are the cardinal directions and their intermediate points. To find stars, hold the map overhead and orient it so one of the labels matches the direction you’re facing. The stars above the map’s horizon now match what’s in the sky.

The all-sky map shows how the sky looks at:

9 p.m. November 18 p.m. November 157 p.m. November 30

Martin Ratcliffe is a planetarium professional with Evans & Sutherland and enjoys observing from Salt Lake City. Alister Ling, who lives in Edmonton, Alberta, is a longtime watcher of the skies.

#6390. Believing you’ll be remembered after death is linked to better mental health

Believing you'll be remembered after death is linked to better mental health and fewer addictive behaviors, according to new research.

When they think about death, some people picture heaven or another life after this one. Others simply hope to be remembered by family and friends, or through the work they leave behind.

In new research on adults living through a war, only that second hope was linked to better mental health.

Those who expected to live on in other people’s memories reported less depression, anxiety and trouble sleeping, while belief in an afterlife showed no link to those problems.

The associations were generally modest, but they appeared across all the mental health and addictive behavior measures examined.

Psychologists Uri Lifshin and Mario Mikulincer led the work at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Both are part of the university’s Israel Center for Addiction and Mental Health.

Lifshin’s team surveyed 2,912 Jewish adults in Israel in February 2025, during the country’s war with Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Everyone answered once, so the survey can show which feelings tend to appear together but not which one comes first.

“The feeling that our lives matter and will continue to matter to other people may be an important part of how we cope with uncertainty and the knowledge of our own mortality,” the researchers wrote.

In his 1973 book The Denial of Death, Ernest Becker wrote that much of human behavior is driven by a need to keep the terror of death out of mind. His ideas grew into terror management theory.

The theory holds that people manage that fear by feeling valued, loved and part of something that will continue after they’re gone.

In tests of the theory, reminders of death have made people more likely to choose alcohol over a nonalcoholic drink.

Similar reminders have raised cravings for tobacco and cannabis. They can also increase the urge to gamble in people who already have a gambling problem.

A 2024 review that pooled 104 studies found a moderate link between fear of death and a range of mental health symptoms.

Psychologists have a name for the opposite feeling, the sense that some part of a person will carry on through other people, a legacy or a group. They call it symbolic immortality.

In an earlier study, Lifshin and colleagues linked that feeling to higher self-esteem. Apart from depression, though, no study had tested whether it was linked to fewer mental health problems or addictive behaviors.

Lifshin’s team collected the answers online, in Hebrew, as the fifth round of a larger national study of mental health and addiction. Volunteers were 18 to 70 years old.

The team built the sample to match Jewish adults in Israel by gender, age, how religious they were and where they lived. Of 10,869 people invited, 4,731 agreed to take part.

The team then dropped incomplete, careless and duplicate answers, along with anyone beyond the sample’s quotas, leaving 2,912.

At the center of it all was a single question. “Do you think that you will be remembered by other people after you die (e.g., through your accomplishments or legacy)?”

Answers ran from 1, for certainly not, to 7, for certainly yes. Most people chose answers toward the yes end of the scale, and the average was 4.55.

Volunteers were also asked whether they believed in an afterlife, such as heaven or reincarnation.

Standard questionnaires covered depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep and emotional control, plus nine kinds of addictive behavior, from problem drinking to social media.

A correlation measures how closely two things are related. Values range from -1 to 1, with zero indicating no linear relationship.

The team adjusted its figures for other differences between people, such as gender, education, politics, military service, relationships, parenthood and afterlife belief.

After that, the hope of being remembered was most closely tied to feeling that life has meaning, at 0.45.

Self-esteem and feeling supported by others each came in at 0.35.

People who expected to be remembered also reported fewer mental health problems. The correlations had magnitudes of 0.27 for trouble managing emotions and 0.26 for depression.

Links of that size reflect a tendency across thousands of people, not a rule for any one person.

Parents, and people in long-term relationships, were slightly more likely to expect to be remembered. Age made no difference.

People who expected to be remembered reported fewer signs of all nine problem habits the survey covered.

The associations were weakest for gambling (0.07) and alcohol (0.08). Internet addiction showed the strongest association (0.18), followed closely by pornography and social media.

“Our findings suggest that feeling connected to others, having meaning in life and believing that something of us will remain may go hand in hand with better mental health and fewer problematic addictive behaviors,” the researchers wrote.

The authors offered one possible reason for the overlap. Other animals can show addictive behaviors, they wrote, but don’t normally develop problem substance use in the wild.

Perhaps, they suggested, that’s because addictions are partly tied to problems only humans face, such as knowing they will die.

The two beliefs did overlap. People who expected to be remembered were also somewhat more likely to believe in an afterlife, with a link of 0.37.

Belief in an afterlife, though, was tied mostly to religion. It was most closely linked to belief in God or a higher power, at 0.79.

Afterlife belief showed no significant association with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep problems or emotional control.

It was associated with slightly less problem drinking, cannabis use, pornography use and compulsive sexual behavior, and slightly more problem internet use.

Even with afterlife belief taken into account, the hope of being remembered kept its links. The study doesn’t show that this hope adds anything beyond self-esteem, meaning or close relationships, though.

The authors describe it instead as a broad marker tied to several of those supports.

Which comes first is the biggest open question. Feeling remembered could help protect mental health, but depression or addiction could also weaken a person’s sense that their life will matter, and each may affect the other.

The hope of being remembered was also measured with one question. The authors wrote that a single item may be less accurate and less stable than a full set.

Timing may matter too. The authors suggested that wartime may have made the links stronger than they would be in peacetime or in other countries.

During a war, they wrote, threat, national identity and trauma are likely to be on many people’s minds.

Everyone in the survey came from the general public rather than from people being treated for addiction or mental illness.

Whether a stronger sense of legacy can actually ease depression or addiction is still unknown.

Answering that will take experiments and long-term studies that follow the same people over time, the authors wrote, along with fuller measures of legacy and repeat surveys in other countries.

The full study was published in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction.

#6389. The 7 Best Pocket Knives for Everyday Tasks and Outdoor Adventures

Our favorite folders, flippers, and automatics from Benchmade, CRKT, Case, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.

Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.

This guide focuses on functional folding knives with (mostly) approachable price tags that you’ll want to use every day, not place under glass. I test dozens of knives each year, and I’ve chosen my favorites below only from the knives I’ve personally used.

The Iridium is one of Kershaw’s most popular releases and for good reason. It’s priced modestly with a secure bar lock-out, easy one-handed opening and closing, and it just looks cool. It’s also the sweet spot for most people in terms of size, weight, and style. Not ultralight (just over three ounces), the 6061-T6’s aluminum handle and slim profile keep it barely noticeable in your pocket.

When testing, I found the 4.5-inch length was great for my medium-sized hands and shouldn’t be too big or small for any hands—or jobs. Kershaw offers low- and mid-priced production knives made in China, but they follow up with high-quality control in their Oregon facilities and consistently deliver designs that just work.

At the core of the Iridium series is a secure, Benchmade-style crossbar lock, and while there are models that veer into Benchmade prices, many models, including the original, can be had for less than $100.

The Iridium is easy to use—opening with a smooth action, activated by the thumb stud opener. Though it’s not spring-assisted, the blade flicks open fast without resistance. Closing is similarly smooth—just pull down on the crossbar lock and close with a finger, or hold upright and let the blade fall shut. I usually prefer the satisfying speed of a flipper, but the smooth action of the Iridium’s thumb stud opening rivals the Benchmade Bugout’s, and it quickly grew on me.

The D2 steel used in the original, which offers decent edge retention and durability, is common in lower-cost knives but can rust if you abuse it. A compromise option: Go with the black oxide-coated D2 blade which keeps all but the cutting edge sealed off from rust. The look on all these versions of the Iridium matches the modern design features, and the only drawback of how smooth and slick the knife looks is that it’s not the best for operating in wet or muddy conditions where grip could become an issue.

Coast is one of several Oregon-based knife manufacturers (the company also sells a wide range of flashlights and headlamps) to offer a range of budget-friendly folding pocket knives. My favorite from their lineup is the fairly small but robust Contra, which has an all-metal build and a lifetime warranty despite the low cost. The wharncliffe blade, made from a softer 7CR17 steel, dulls faster than high-end steels but has the benefit of being easy to sharpen at home.

The wharncliffe blade gives you the utility of a box cutter blade but much more versatility as you retain a decent point for puncturing tasks, and I’ve come to prefer it for everyday carry over more traditional drop point shapes. Coast adds durability to its budget steel with a black oxide coating that I found doesn’t scratch easily. The knife is a full stainless-steel build with a good-looking stonewash finish on the handle which integrates the frame lock system.

The flipper opening is fast and satisfying for knife fidgeters but it’s usually safer to employ a two-handed closure. Given the overseas production and ultra-low sticker price, this pocket knife’s durability could be a potential concern, but I’ve used mine roughly near-daily for more than a year and haven’t broken or chipped the blade. It still looks new.

Case is one of the original American knife brands still standing and, unlike many of their competitors that have shipped production to China, most of Case’s knives are still designed and produced in Bradford, Pennsylvania.

Whether or not that matters to you, Case makes great knives, and while they sell a lot of nostalgic designs unchanged for a century, the Kinzua is one of their modern EDC offerings that departs from the Case aesthetic with an all-metal build, flipper action, sharp lines, and a tanto blade.

The satin-finished S35VN steel blade is a good compromise of hardness and edge durability while still being fairly easy to sharpen at home. It also has a lightly weathered look that should hide abuse well. One note is that, while extremely sturdy, the all-metal frame-lock design is pretty stiff to close out of the box.

Releasing the frame lock requires some force and closing requires a few moves. With a little practice I was able to comfortably operate it one-handed, but folks with smaller or weaker hands may not feel the same.

Benchmade is an American knife brand based in Oregon with a loyal following for its premium production pocket knives. Known for lightweight designs, modern materials, and innovation, the brand has produced many favorites—but my top pick is the Benchmade 535 Bugout.

To me, the Bugout captures what Benchmade does best: an ultralight folder that’s still strong, well-built, and made with high-quality steel (and the same holds true with the Benchmade 533 Mini Bugout). Some might argue the Benchmade Osborne 940 is the brand’s most iconic knife, but I reach for the Bugout every time—especially for hunting, camping, backpacking, or backcountry skiing, where weight matters.

The design is modern without feeling overly tactical. It’s streamlined with a simple profile and a practical drop-point blade. The textured Grivory scales—glass-reinforced plastic—keep weight incredibly low while maintaining rigidity.

At under two ounces and just 0.42 inches thick, the Bugout is barely noticeable in a pocket, making it ideal for long outdoor trips. For those who don’t like the Grivory feel, there are versions with aluminum or carbon-fiber scales and a range of steel options.

Operation is another highlight. Benchmade’s Axis Lock uses a spring-loaded crossbar that allows easy one-handed opening and closing from either hand while keeping fingers out of the blade path. The mechanism is simple, strong, and easy to maintain—I even built one myself at the Benchmade factory and found it intuitive without instructions.

In terms of cutting performance, my Bugouts arrived razor-sharp out of the box. I prefer the standard S30V steel because it balances edge retention with easier sharpening in the field, though higher-end options like S90V are available if you want longer-lasting sharpness. S30V is also tough and corrosion-resistant, which suits hard outdoor use.

Benchmade’s lifetime warranty and sharpening service add real long-term value. The Bugout isn’t cheap, but with its reliability, ultralight design, and customization options, it’s easy to recommend—especially for outdoor enthusiasts or anyone wanting a high-quality everyday carry knife.

The Bugout is one of our favorite Benchmade folders, and we recommend it above as our Best Lightweight pocket knife. But the brand’s new Bugout Vapyr variant is different enough to warrant its own place on the podium. The most noticeable difference is the width. The original Bugout is featherlight at two ounces, but the Vapyr gets that down to 1.72 ounces and shrinks the width by 3 mm, which is very obvious in the hand.

It’s impressive engineering, but practically, it takes a knife that was barely noticeable in the pocket and makes it borderline undetectable. It costs $375—nearly double the regular Bugout—so this is for folks with fewer budget constraints who are willing to spend for the lightest, thinnest folder that doesn’t compromise on utility and durability.

Part of that price jump can be chalked up to Benchmade swapping in MagnaCut steel for the S30V in the baseline Bugout. S30V is already a great blade steel with high corrosion resistance and incredible edge retention, and Benchmade has come to be known for using it. But MagnaCut is a step above on both metrics.

The other big change is the Axis lock, which remains functionally the same but swaps in a new stepped slide in place of the longstanding metal button. It’s a minor swap that first-time Benchmade buyers likely won’t even notice. But having used Axis locks for years, I much prefer the new slide.

There’s a subtle internal change from an omega spring to a tension spring. It didn’t feel different when I used it side by side with the original Bugout, but Benchmade says the tension springs have a longer lifespan. It’s worth noting that while better durability is welcome considering the price tag, all Benchmade knives have a lifetime warranty (and lifetime sharpening service) if a spring were to fail.

One drawback from the original Bugout is that, at least with the Bugout Vapyr I tested, the pivot is much tighter and requires more force to open. You can open a Bugout one of two ways. One, you can use the thumb stud to spin the blade out into the locked-open position. Alternatively, you can pull the Axis lock open and flick the blade open. This second option requires a touch of timing and gets harder with the Vapyr’s tighter pivot, though I didn’t find the thumb stud actuation any more challenging in the Vapyr.

I’ve been looking for a good automatic pocket knife for years, and the CRKT Twist Tighe Automatic is the only one that I’ve found that doesn't feel like a novelty knife. It’s compact, lightweight, fun to use, and practical enough for everyday carry while still delivering the fun factor that draws many people to automatic knives in the first place.

Automatics, often called switchblades, are popular with knife enthusiasts because they’re inherently fidget-friendly. The Twist Tighe is an out-the-front (OTF) automatic, meaning the blade deploys straight out of the front of the handle. Besides being undeniably cool, I find the operation safer than many folding knives because it’s harder to accidentally place your fingers in the blade’s path when opening and closing.

The highlight is its smooth double-action mechanism. Sliding the spine button forward fires the blade; pulling it back retracts it. Many automatics I’ve tried are either stiff or inconsistent, but the Twist Tighe feels smooth and reliable even after repeated use. That ease of operation also makes it surprisingly approachable for people who aren’t experienced with knives.

The design comes from Canadian knife designer Brian Tighe, and the handle’s raised spiral grooves are a distinctive touch fans of his work will recognize. In the all-black configuration, the knife looks sleek and slightly dramatic without becoming impractical. My version features a tanto blade with a black titanium nitride finish, while other configurations of the Twist Tighe have double-edged blades and more colorful scale options.

Size and weight are also big differences from other automatics. At just 1.6 ounces with a 2.65-inch blade and about a 4-inch closed length, it’s remarkably small for an OTF knife and easy to carry daily. However, people with large hands may find it a bit compact.

Overall, the Twist Tighe combines premium materials like CPM MagnaCut steel with one of the smoothest actions I’ve experienced. If you’re looking for a compact, high-quality OTF automatic for everyday carry, it’s an excellent choice.

The CRKT Minimalist Nessmuk combines the classic look of an outdoor blade with everyday convenience—plus there are several carry options for its sheath. It’s also surprisingly affordable for the build quality, priced at well under $100, with 12C27 stainless steel that keeps the cost down while providing corrosion resistance and easy sharpening.

Another thing in its favor is its versatility beyond hunting season. Thanks to its broad belly, it excels at slicing food, carving wood, breaking down cardboard, and cutting cordage.

With three deep finger choils in the G10 handle, it remained comfortable in hand while I tested it, and the textured scales provided better grip than many larger knives with smoother handles. That may not be the case for folks with larger hands, however, considering the size of the handle. Still, for most people, it’s an excellent choice for a fixed blade that can handle general tasks.

Testing and reviewing knives is a mostly subjective affair, despite all the ink spilled over steel hardness and the trade-offs between edge retention and durability. And with that in mind, I should highlight that these selections are made by one person and thus subject to my personal biases when it comes to pocket knives.

While I’ve developed many idiosyncratic preferences over more than a decade of knife reviewing and 40 years plus of knife-using, the big one is that I am a knife user before a knife enthusiast. I can appreciate a “cool” knife design as much as any other knife nut that owns hundreds of knives, but I’m partial to folding designs that work well, fit my hand, and make my life easier in their role as an essential daily use tool.

We update this guide multiple times throughout the year, and I’m constantly testing new pocket knives to look for new models that are worthy enough to unseat the favorites—and I don’t do that lightly. Year-round testing allows for longer-term use instead of a couple days of fidgeting with a blade and writing up a review. Most of the pocket knives featured here have been in my pocket on and off for months if not years, tackling everyday tasks as well as seasonal jobs such as butchering an elk or deer (if I’m lucky). We’ve included knives from the downright cheap to prohibitively expensive, but all the knives featured are ones we feel deliver good value considering the price tier.

As a baseline for any new knife, I check the factory edge for sharpness, look for corrosion resistance with a saltwater bath and air drying, and (when feasible) disassemble the knife to better understand the lock and open/close mechanisms. After beating up a knife for a while, I also sharpen the blade with stones with an angle guide to find out just how easy it is to return the blade to sharp. One of my favorite tests is handing a knife to friends and strangers to see how regular people react to opening and closing one for the first time, since I spend more time with knives than most.

Choosing blade steel is where knife geeks can get into the weeds. There are trade-offs, though, with any type of steel. Broadly speaking, if you go with a softer steel it means the blade may get dull more easily but it's also easier to sharpen. Harder types of steel hold an edge longer but might be trickier for novices to sharpen at home.

Steel characteristics also affect how prone a blade will be to rusting; however, most decent modern pocket knives use a steel that’s rust-resistant enough that it won't require lots of special care. Almost all knives’ product pages will list the type of steel used, and if they don’t, it’s likely a budget knife. If you can’t find the steel online, check knife marketplace sites such as BladeHQ for the make and model.

Here are the highlights for some of the more common pocket knife steel types:

Handle material is also an important choice. Wood is less common these days and less durable than steel or lighter, more durable synthetic materials like G10 and carbon fiber. Still, you may prefer the feel and look of wood despite the drawbacks. Steel is strong and durable but adds weight which can be a positive or a negative depending on how you use the knife and what you prefer hanging on your pocket.

A knife’s dimensions and weight affect the fit in your hand and ease of use. In general, bigger hands won’t like tiny knives and vice versa, but how and where you carry a knife impact your preferences for size and weight. If you’re an office executive, you may not want an oversized, obvious blade for daily carry, while working on a farm or in the trades, you might prefer a bigger, burlier blade to stand up to prying tasks and day-to-day abuse.

The action of a pocket knife can play an outsized role in your appreciation for it. I routinely test a lot of folding knives and find the knives I reach for most often are ones that are the most (subjectively) satisfying—and that I can easily operate one-handed when my off hand is busy doing something else. If you carry it long enough, you’ll get proficient with most any knife, but each of these common mechanisms has its strengths and weaknesses to consider.

In the previous century, secure locking mechanisms weren’t common, but today they’re expected if not universal. Classic knives, such as Case’s beloved Stockman and Victorinox’s iconic Swiss Army Knife, use slip joints, which hold the blade open but don’t truly lock. Because of the increased safety of a locking blade, I recommend choosing a pocket knife with some kind of a locking mechanism. If you are comfortable with a slip joint or other non-locking blade and enjoy the style, by all means, buy one. Note that your choice of lock typically dictates how you close the knife, so this will have a major impact on how easy it is to operate.

If cost is a major factor for you, it will quickly narrow the range of options. Knives can range in cost from just a few dollars to hundreds or even thousands for custom and limited edition options from celebrated knifemakers. Most people, however, will be looking at what are called “production knives”—models that are mass-produced, usually in a factory instead of by hand from individual knifemakers. While these blades can still run up to $500 or so, the range is much tighter as the cost to produce is lower.

Knives for less than about $20 will usually feature softer, cheaper steels and inexpensive handles. These knives may have less quality control than pricier models, but you can still get a decent knife from an established manufacturer any day of the week for less than $50. For example, the cheapest knife I recommend costs about $25.

Choosing a pocket knife with harder carbon steel will usually push the price closer to $100 or more. Go past that $100 price point, and you’re paying for specific designs, brand names, and other personal preferences, but you’ll start to see diminishing returns as far as raw functionality.

In the United States, carrying most pocket knives won’t break any laws. But each state has its own rules that might restrict the specific pocket knives you can legally carry. Many states have prohibitions on certain automatic knives, on blade length, and even on whether or not you can carry certain knives concealed.

The American Knife and Tool Institute has a helpful state-by-state guide to knife laws you can consult. Traveling abroad brings an even wider range of regulations, as some countries such as Austria have almost no restrictions while Norway (despite a rich knifemaking heritage) has an outright ban on carrying knives in urban areas.

Possibly. First, not all pocket knives are the same. The legal definition of pocket knives may vary across states and at the federal level which can impact shipment and receipt.

Most states also have some kind of restrictions on what knives you can carry on your person. Even in wild west Colorado where I live, it is illegal to carry a blade longer than 3.5 inches “concealed” which would include “in your pocket.” In New York state where I grew up, switchblades are illegal and you must be a U.S. citizen to even own a knife, but there are no concealed carry restrictions. Check your state laws here.

Outside of local laws, consider how a knife fits in your hand. A knife that feels tiny and awkward to someone with large hands might be perfect for someone else. If you’re not already a regular pocket knife carrier, stop into an outdoors store where you can handle a wide range of knives and see what feels good. Most people will feel comfortable with blades in the 2.5- to 3-inch range, though folks with larger hands may want something bigger.

I’ll start with a caution—that you may not want a surgically sharp pocket knife. Because I use my pocket knife so frequently and casually, I don’t like to be as cautious as you have to be with an ultra-sharp blade.

I experimented with carrying a replaceable blade knife for a few months and I ended up giving myself several minor but annoying slices. That said, any knife will eventually require sharpening. Most pocket knives have a fairly obtuse 20-degree or higher blade angle, which makes them less challenging to sharpen yourself.

Knife sharpening is a skill that’s not easy to master (learn how here), but there are tools available to help. While whetstone sharpening is soothing in a Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance sort of way, you probably already have a pull-through sharpener somewhere (check kitchen drawers).

These sharpeners aren’t the perfect sharpening solution, but they’re relatively idiot-proof and good enough to perk up your blade. If all of this sounds like something you’ll never bother with, there are lots of mail-in sharpening services such as The Sharp Brothers, who will professionally sharpen your blades for a fee. Also, many manufacturers offer similar services. Benchmade, for example, has a LifeSharp program that gives you free sharpening for any Benchmade knife. Some manufacturers such as Kershaw also offer blade replacement (often for a fee) if you’ve broken or otherwise damaged your blade beyond repair.

This is both a surprisingly common and difficult-to-answer question. Obviously personal budget comes into play, but so do your preferences. Despite considering myself a pocket knife enthusiast, I carried a cheap pocket knife from Walmart for years that cost me literally $1. The company raised the price to $2 at some point. Those knives would rust at the hinge, but they did the trick and were great for putting in my checked luggage. I wouldn’t worry about losing it at my destination and wouldn’t cry if the TSA took it.

While I can’t recommend buying $2 knives in good conscience for most circumstances, quality options such as the Coast Contra recommended above can be had for under $20. If you’re new to knives, start out with something cheaper, definitely under $50, until you develop strong opinions about the pocket knife you prefer.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. She spent more than a decade as a staff editor and writer at TripAdvisor and Penguin Random House and her byline has appeared in Time Out New York, the New York Daily News, and New York Magazine. #6388. Did viruses borrow their shells from bacteria? New evidence raises questions

Tiny viruses found in gut DNA carry a virus protein shell much like the boxes bacteria use for chemistry, and the design crossed both ways.

Many viruses have a remarkably simple design: a protein shell containing their genetic material.

Bacteria build almost the same shell and use it as a sealed container for chemical reactions, with enzymes inside instead of genes. For years the leading idea was that bacteria had borrowed the design from viruses.

Now a search through billions of DNA fragments has turned up tiny viruses whose shell proteins look more like the bacterial version.

The family tree they belong to runs in both directions. The researchers found evidence that the shell may have passed between viruses and cells at least three times, in both directions.

Abelardo Aguilar, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami, led the search with Antoni Luque, an associate professor of biology there.

The team never grew a single virus. Everything came from DNA sequences in public databases, read from soil, seawater, wastewater, and the human gut.

“The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab,” Luque said.

“But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don’t know the host, that we can’t culture in the lab, but that are everywhere.”

The protein at the center of the story folds into a shape biologists call the HK97 fold, and copies of it assemble into hollow shells.

In a large family of viruses, that shell is the capsid, the case around the genome.

In bacteria and in archaea, a separate branch of single-celled life, the same fold builds a container called an encapsulin, which cells use to store iron and run other chemistry.

The two versions differ in size. Most encapsulins are built from 60 copies of the protein.

Many viral capsids are larger and have additional assembly machinery, including scaffolds, DNA-packaging portals, and sometimes tails.

The size gap is the problem with the old story. If encapsulins came from viruses, the simpler structure evolved from the more complex one, and that idea never said how.

Aguilar’s team reasoned that if the two shells were related, there might be viruses nobody had found yet, small enough to sit between them.

The smallest known tailed virus of this family has a genome 11,600 base pairs long, the paired letters that DNA is written in.

The team sifted more than 14.4 billion DNA fragments, including those in IMG/M, run by the Department of Energy’s Joint Genome Institute.

They kept only fragments that looked like complete viral genomes, carried this virus family’s hallmark genes, and fell below that line. That left 4,730 candidate genomes.

Each genome’s shell protein was then checked against the sequence signatures of encapsulins, with AlphaFold and other AI tools predicting the proteins’ shapes.

Among the genomes between 5,000 and 11,600 letters long, 93 of 491 shell proteins, nearly 19%, carried encapsulin signatures. In a control set of slightly larger viral genomes, 2.5% did.

The biggest cluster of these encapsulin-like viruses, 76 of the 93, came from human gut samples. Their genomes averaged about 8,750 letters.

None carried a portal, a tail, or the motor that known viruses of this family use to pack DNA into the shell.

Genes they did carry included ones for splicing themselves into a host bacterium’s chromosome and lying dormant there.

So how do these viruses copy themselves with no portal? The authors suggested they may depend on other viruses for the missing parts, or may carry single-stranded DNA and pack it through pores in the shell.

Several of their genes fit the second idea, though it remains untested, the team wrote.

The team built family trees of the HK97 fold three ways, from the proteins’ sequences, from their predicted shapes, and from which features they share.

All three methods produced groups in which viruses and encapsulins sat side by side.

In one group, a family of encapsulins clustered with viruses that infect soil bacteria.

In another, a virus that infects archaea clustered with an archaeal encapsulin rather than with other viruses.

At least three separate crossings, in the team’s reading, and not all in the same direction.

A capsid is built in stages. The shell proteins first assemble around the scaffold into a smaller, empty form called a procapsid.

As the genome is packaged, the procapsid expands and matures into the finished viral shell.

Aguilar’s team compared a bacterial encapsulin with a procapsid and finished capsid from a Staphylococcus aureus genetic element.

The two proteins share only 14% of their sequence. Yet the encapsulin and the procapsid are almost the same size inside, about 1.3 millionths of an inch (33 nanometers) across.

Inside an encapsulin sits an enzyme. Inside a procapsid sits the scaffold, and the two proteins turned out to share a similar helical structure.

So the authors proposed that whatever sits inside the shell decides what the shell becomes. An enzyme turns it into a reactor. A scaffold lets it expand and take on a genome.

“One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole,” Aguilar explained.

The study doesn’t settle whether the first HK97 shell held genes or enzymes.

The deep branches of the family tree are too poorly supported to say, and the authors wrote that repeated crossings may have erased the signature of the earliest steps.

The authors’ best guess, which they labeled speculative, is that the earliest shells were built from 12 to 24 proteins, too small to hold any genome.

In their model, chemistry came first and genes later, once the shells grew to 60 proteins.

Whether procapsids in living bacteria run reactions during an infection is what no one has measured.

Infected cells often produce empty procapsids, the authors wrote, so a lab could test that directly.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6387. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

#6386. Deep inside a Spanish cave, archaeologists found at least 120 Latin inscriptions, and five of them honor a goddess called ‘the Lady’

At least 120 Latin inscriptions in Cova Dones, Spain, name a goddess called Domina, the Lady, and point to women taking an active part in her cult.

One chamber of Cova Dones, a cave in Millares in Valencia province, now holds at least 120 Latin inscriptions. Teams from the universities of Alicante and Zaragoza recorded them during fieldwork in May and June 2026.

When the room was first explored in 2024, about 15 had been logged.

Five of the texts are vows to Domina, “the Lady,” a goddess the visitors addressed with reverence. Several of the names read so far are women’s. The team calls the results preliminary, and many texts are still being read.

The researchers call the room the Roman Sanctuary. It sits more than 650 feet (200 meters) from the entrance, according to the University of Alicante.

Most of the texts are believed to date to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, and they cover the walls and the ceiling. Small natural pools on the floor, known as gours, catch water from the galleries, and visitors dropped offerings into them.

That first campaign also yielded a coin from the reign of Emperor Claudius. Someone had wedged it as an offering between a fissure and a stalactite in the ceiling, and in a team photo Xabier Garín Artázcoz points at the crack. Trinidad Pasíes Oviedo of the Valencia Museum of Prehistory recovered and conserved the coin.

The January 2025 announcement from the University of Alicante placed the room among the deepest known Roman inscription sites in Iberia, second only to Cueva del Puente in Burgos and possibly Cueva de Román de Clunia.

This year’s readings were done by two epigraphy specialists. Silvia Alfayé teaches ancient history at the University of Zaragoza, and Sergio García-Dils lectures at UNED in Seville. García-Dils also directs the Spanish School of Speleology.

According to Alfayé, five votive texts show that women “played an active role in her cult.” Three of them carry the word MALACI. In a release dated July 27, the University of Alicante called it an unpublished epithet for a goddess not known until now.

García-Dils noted that the texts are packed into one marked-off part of the cave, well away from the entrance. To him that “strongly suggests the existence of a well-organised and structured cult” with a named deity, not scattered visits.

The University of Southampton, where Aitor Ruiz-Redondo is also based, put out the English release on October 20. It says early readings suggest some women wrote their vows themselves, without a go-between.

Until now, the Roman cave sanctuary with the largest known set of inscriptions was La Griega, with 107. One of them names a woman.

The 2026 team logged objects on the chamber floor, among them two bronze rings found under the inscribed rock. There were two bronze rings, a bracelet, chalice-shaped cups, spindle whorls, bits of pottery and animal bones.

The whorls came up in numbers. Virginia Barciela co-leads the project with Ruiz-Redondo and teaches prehistory at Alicante. She said the whorls probably point to offerings of spindles, a textile tool tied to women in antiquity.

She also brought up the first written name of the site, Cova de les Dones, meaning Cave of the Women. That name may hold “the fossilised memory of a place long associated with women,” she said, or with female spirits.

Alfayé said the goddess’s title may have to do with water. Water shrines existed elsewhere in the ancient world, such as a circular water shrine at Pelusium in northern Sinai.

The inscriptions are extremely difficult to see with the naked eye. So the team photographed the surfaces for high-resolution photogrammetric models and read the texts on those.

That work turned up inscriptions no one had seen. It also split apart lines that earlier readers had taken as one text.

Jorge Angás and Carlos Valladares, from the IPH institute in Zaragoza and the DigHER project, ran the geomatics side. Javier Velaza Frías, a Latin professor in Barcelona, leads the study of the Roman inscriptions. Víctor Sabaté Vidal of the University of Valencia has also contributed to the project.

Latin wishes turn up on other Roman objects too, for instance openwork glass cups carved with drinking wishes in Greek or Latin.

In a Roman underground sanctuary, finding texts and offerings together in place is exceptionally rare, says the Southampton release.

Ruiz-Redondo, Barciela and archaeologist Ximo Martorell published the first results in 2023. In the journal Antiquity they described over 100 Paleolithic paintings and engravings. Some are older than 24,000 years.

Pottery from the Iron Age had already led archaeologists in the 1960s to class it as an Iberian sanctuary. In 2025 the team logged more than 100 stalagmites that people had modified on purpose.

For that kind of find, the University of Alicante ranks the cave second in the world, after Saint-Marcel in France.

Ruiz-Redondo said people may have kept returning for “its permanent water supply,” its landscape or its easy access.

At La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales, red marks have been dated to more than 64,000 years ago.

Alfayé and her colleagues are still working on the goddess’s title. For now the team has not said who Domina was or what MALACI means. Many inscriptions are still being read, and much of the cave is unstudied, so 120 is a minimum.

The DONARQ project started in 2023 with money from the Generalitat Valenciana and the British Academy. In September 2026 the sanctuary was shortlisted for a National Geographic +Historia readers’ prize. Public voting closed on October 12.

This year the regional Pla Restaura program and the Millares town council are paying for more work. The money goes to the cave’s access and entrance, safety measures, a digital twin and a catalog of the Paleolithic images. The company Arquivolta Patrimoni i Societat is coordinating it, and virtual visits should follow.

Among those offerings, two bronze rings sat on the surface right below the inscribed rock.

The information was obtained from the University of Southampton , the University of Alicante and the University of Zaragoza.

#6385. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 1: The Moon in Cancer

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time this morning, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early this morning, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

The Moon will reach Last Quarter phase this afternoon at 3:28 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:29 A.M.Sunset: 4:57 P.M.Moonrise: 11:23 P.M.Moonset: 1:11 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (47%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

By 5 A.M. local time on November 2, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter. The gas giant is by far the brightest light here, shining at magnitude –2.0. This morning it lies halfway between the Moon and Regulus to its lower left (east), Leo’s alpha star and the base of the Sickle asterism.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time. Make sure to check out the view tomorrow for comparison.
